body:
## Problem

`computeIntersection` builds the conjunction of N ranges by string-joining them (`intersect.ts:96` `combined = ${combined} ${entry.range}`, and `intersect.ts:112` `simplified.join(' ')`). In semver grammar `||` binds looser than the space (AND) operator, so joining `A || B` with `C` yields `A || (B C)`, not `(A || B) && C`. Any input range containing `||` produces a semantically wrong result — the tool's single headline output.

## Evidence

Ran against the real implementation:

    computeIntersection([{range: '^17 || ^18'}, {range: '^16 || ^18'}])
    -> ">=16.0.0 <17.0.0-0 || >=18.0.0 <18.0.0-0 || >=18.0.0 <19.0.0-0"
       16.5.0: reported=true  truth=false   <<< WRONG

    computeIntersection([{range: '^14 || ^16 || ^18'}, {range: '^16 || ^18 || ^20'}])
    -> ">=14.0.0 <15.0.0-0 || >=16.0.0 <17.0.0-0 || >=18.0.0 <17.0.0-0 || ..."
       14.1.0: reported=true truth=false   <<< WRONG
       20.1.0: reported=true truth=false   <<< WRONG

The emitted string even contains the unsatisfiable group `>=18.0.0 <17.0.0-0`, proving the reconstruction is malformed rather than merely imprecise.

## Impact

`^18 || ^19` style peer ranges are the norm for react/vue/webpack, and `^18 || ^20 || ^22` is the norm for `engines.node`. For any such input the tool reports node/peer versions as safe that satisfy only one input constraint. A user who pins CI to a version the tool blessed gets a broken install. This is the product's core claim.

## Fix

Never concatenate range strings. Build the conjunction with semver's own range algebra, distributing the AND over each OR-set:

    import semver from 'semver'
    function andRanges(a: string, b: string): string | null {
      const out: string[] = []
      for (const ga of new semver.Range(a).set)
        for (const gb of new semver.Range(b).set) {
          const g = [...ga, ...gb].map(c => c.value).filter(v => v !== '').join(' ') || '*'
          if (semver.validRange(g) !== null && semver.subset(g, g)) out.push(g)
        }
      const joined = out.join(' || ')
      return semver.validRange(joined)
    }

then fold with `andRanges` instead of template-string concatenation, and drop OR-groups that are empty (`semver.minVersion(group) === null`). Feed the per-group result through `simplifyComparators` (which already operates per-group and is correct) before joining with `||`. Regression test: assert `semver.satisfies(v, result) === (satisfies(v, r1) && satisfies(v, r2))` for every `v` in a sampled set, over inputs containing `||`.

## Resolution
Replaced string-concatenation with andRanges() in src/analyzer/intersect.ts: the AND is distributed across both OR-sets and groups whose semver.minVersion() is null (unsatisfiable) are dropped. filterSubsumed deleted - the fold now produces the tightest result directly. Verified: ['^17 || ^18','^16 || ^18'] now yields '>=18.0.0 <19.0.0-0' (was admitting 16.5.0). 9 new semantic tests in test/analyzer/intersect.test.ts assert satisfies(v,result) === every(satisfies(v,input)) over a 10-version sample, plus a test that no unsatisfiable OR-group is ever emitted.
title: OR-ranges corrupted by string concatenation; wrong safe range reported

## Problem

`resolveLocal` looks up `node_modules/<name>/package.json` by name only (`local.ts:18`, `local.ts:34`) and applies the result to every `Package` with that name. A lockfile legitimately contains several versions of the same package; node_modules holds exactly one hoisted copy. Every non-hoisted version gets the hoisted version's `engines` and `peerDependencies`.

## Evidence

Ran the real function against a temp project whose node_modules holds `foo@3.0.0` with `engines.node: ">=20"`:

    resolveLocal([{name:'foo',version:'3.0.0'}, {name:'foo',version:'1.0.0'}], dir)
    -> [{"name":"foo","version":"3.0.0","engines":{"node":">=20"}},
        {"name":"foo","version":"1.0.0","engines":{"node":">=20"}}]

`foo@1.0.0` is reported as requiring node >=20 purely because 3.0.0 is hoisted. Pass 1 runs before the registry pass, and `client.ts:122` only overwrites when the registry lookup succeeds — so with `--offline`, or on any registry miss, the fabricated constraint survives into the final intersection.

## Impact

Fabricated constraints narrow (or, symmetrically, widen) the computed safe range. In `--offline` mode, which the README advertises as a first-class mode, this is the only data source, so the wrong answer is the only answer.

## Fix

Verify the manifest's version before using it, in `readLocalManifest`'s caller:

    const manifest = readLocalManifest(pkg.name, projectDir)
    if (manifest === null || manifest.version !== pkg.version) return pkg

and add `version?: string` to the `PackageManifest` interface (local.ts:5). Optionally fall back to the nested copy at `node_modules/<parent>/node_modules/<name>/package.json` before giving up. Test: two entries of one name, one version present in node_modules — assert the other keeps `engines === undefined`.

## Resolution
src/registry/local.ts now skips the manifest when manifest.version is a string and differs from pkg.version; added version?: string to PackageManifest. A manifest with no version field still applies (unchanged behaviour). Two tests in test/registry/local.test.ts cover both paths.
title: resolveLocal stamps the hoisted manifest onto every version of a package

## Problem

For pnpm v9 the parser iterates `snapshots` for the package list but looks the metadata up in `packages` using the _unstripped_ snapshot key (`pnpm.ts:65` `const meta = metaBlock[key] ?? {}`). In the v9 format `snapshots` keys carry a peer-resolution suffix — `vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)` — while `packages` keys never do. The lookup misses and `meta` falls back to `{}`. `extractNameVersion` already strips the suffix at `pnpm.ts:26`; the metadata lookup does not.

## Evidence

Ran the real parser on a minimal v9 lockfile where `packages` declares `engines: { node: '>=18' }` and `peerDependencies: { vue: ^3.2.0 }` for `vue-router@4.2.5`, and `snapshots` keys it as `vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)`:

    parsePnpmLockfile(yaml)
    -> [{"name":"vue-router","version":"4.2.5"}]      // engines/peerDependencies gone

The committed fixture `test/fixtures/pnpm-lock-v9.yaml` has no peer-suffixed snapshot keys, so the whole test suite passes over this path.

## Impact

Every peer-dependent package in a real pnpm v9 lockfile — which is exactly the population whose `peerDependencies` this tool exists to analyze — contributes no constraints. With `--offline` nothing recovers them and the reported safe range is silently too permissive.

## Fix

Strip the suffix before the metadata lookup:

    const stripped = key.replace(/\([^)]*\)/gu, '').trim()
    const meta = metaBlock[stripped] ?? metaBlock[key] ?? {}

Add a peer suffix to `test/fixtures/pnpm-lock-v9.yaml` (e.g. a `vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)` snapshot entry backed by a plain `packages` entry with `engines`) and assert engines survive.

## Resolution
src/parsers/pnpm.ts strips the peer-resolution suffix before the metadata lookup: metaBlock[strippedKey] ?? metaBlock[key] ?? {}. Two tests in test/parsers/pnpm.test.ts use a v9 lockfile whose snapshot key is 'vue-router@4.2.5(vue@3.3.4)' and assert engines and peerDependencies both survive.
title: pnpm v9: engines and peerDependencies dropped for peer-suffixed snapshots

body:
## Problem

Every registry failure path returns `null` and is discarded: `client.ts:58` (`if (!res.ok) return null`), `client.ts:66` (`catch { return null }`), and the same pair at `client.ts:91`/`client.ts:101`. `processBatch` then falls back to whatever was already on the package (`client.ts:122-123`), which for yarn and npm-v1 lockfiles is `undefined`. Nothing counts, reports, or surfaces the failures.

## Impact

Missing constraint data is indistinguishable from "no constraint declared". Because the output is an _intersection_, dropping constraints can only make the reported range wider — the tool fails open in the direction that produces a falsely reassuring answer. A transient DNS failure, a rate limit (npm returns 429 to unauthenticated bulk clients), or an offline corporate proxy all yield a clean-looking table with no warning. The spinner even prints `Fetching registry data... 214/214` on completion, implying success.

## Evidence

Simulate by pointing at an unreachable registry: every fetch throws, every `catch` returns null, and the run still exits 0 with a rendered table. The existing test `fetchManifest: fetch throws → no crash, package returned unchanged` (test/registry/client.test.ts) asserts exactly this silent behaviour as correct.

## Fix

Thread a failure count through `CacheCounter` (rename to a result accumulator), increment it on every `!res.ok` / `catch`, and have `resolveRegistry` return it. In `cli.ts` after the registry pass, when `failed > 0`, write to stderr:

    console.error(`Warning: ${failed}/${packages.length} packages could not be resolved from the registry; the reported ranges may be too permissive.`)

Also render an explicit `unresolved` count in the `--json` payload so CI consumers can gate on it.

## Resolution
CacheCounter gained a 'failed' field, incremented at every !res.ok / !data.version / catch site in fetchManifest and fetchLatest. resolveRegistry now returns { packages, failed } (ResolveResult) and cli.ts prints a stderr warning naming the count and stating the ranges may be too permissive. Three tests cover non-ok, thrown, and offline. Note: writing these tests caught a real miss - fetchLatest's catch had not been given the increment.
title: Registry failures silently widen the reported safe range

body:
## Problem

Three separate paths that should catch a type or lint error all fail to gate:

1. `ci.yml:33` runs `npm run lint`, which is `prettier --write . && eslint --fix .` (package.json:16). It mutates the checkout and then the workflow discards it. Formatting violations and auto-fixable lint errors are silently repaired and never reported.
2. `.mega-linter.yml` `DISABLE_LINTERS` includes `TYPESCRIPT_ES` and `JAVASCRIPT_ES`, so the PR Lint workflow does not lint TS/JS either.
3. There is no `typecheck` script and no `tsc --noEmit` step. The build is `tsup` (package.json:14), which transpiles via esbuild and performs **no** type checking, and `tsconfig.json` sets `"noEmit": true` so `tsc` is never invoked by the build at all.

## Evidence

`grep -n 'tsc' package.json .github/workflows/*.yml` returns nothing. `tsup.config.ts:8` sets `dts: false`, confirming no `tsc` pass in the bundle step. Locally `npx tsc --noEmit` exits 0 today — but nothing in CI would notice if that changed.

## Impact

A type error, or any lint error a human would have to fix, reaches `main` and then npm via `publish.yml`, which runs `npm run build` with no verification gate. The repo is `strict: true` TypeScript whose strictness is never enforced.

## Fix

Add to package.json scripts:

    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit",
    "lint": "prettier --check . && eslint .",
    "lint:fix": "prettier --write . && eslint --fix ."

and in `ci.yml`, replace the single lint step with:

    - run: npm run lint
    - run: npm run typecheck

Keep `lint:fix` for local use and update the README Development table (README "Development" section) which currently documents `npm run lint` as "Prettier format + ESLint auto-fix".

## Resolution
package.json: 'lint' is now 'prettier --check . && eslint .' (gating), auto-fix moved to 'lint:fix', and a 'typecheck' script runs 'tsc --noEmit'. ci.yml runs lint then typecheck. Verified the new gate works: it immediately failed on an unformatted README during this run. README and CLAUDE.md command tables updated. .mega-linter.yml still disables TYPESCRIPT_ES, which is now correct - ci.yml owns TS linting.
title: No gating lint or typecheck for TypeScript anywhere in CI

## Problem

`buildEdgeMap` derives the node name by stripping only the leading `node_modules/` (`graph/index.ts:44` `key.slice('node_modules/'.length)`). npm v2/v3 lockfiles key non-hoisted packages by their full nested path, so `node_modules/app-dep/node_modules/nested` becomes the node name `app-dep/node_modules/nested`, which no edge list ever references.

## Evidence

Ran the real function on a v3 lockfile with one nested package:

    buildEdgeMap(lock, 'npm')
    -> [ ['app-dep', ['nested']],
         ['app-dep/node_modules/nested', ['deep']],
         ['deep', []] ]

`bfs` (graph/index.ts:107) looks up `'nested'`, finds no entry, and stops. `deep` — reachable in reality only through `nested` — is never visited.

## Impact

`--no-dev` classifies packages by set membership: anything in `devReachable` but not `productionSet` is dropped (graph/index.ts:145-148). A production package reachable only through a non-hoisted intermediate is absent from `productionSet`, so if anything dev-side also reaches it, it is wrongly excluded — and its `engines` constraint vanishes from the intersection, widening the reported safe range.

## Fix

Key by the last path segment, matching `parsers/npm.ts:38-39`:

    const name = key.split('node_modules/').at(-1)
    if (typeof name === 'undefined') continue
    edges.set(name, Object.keys(entry.dependencies ?? {}))

Merge rather than overwrite when the same name appears at several depths, so a nested copy's edges do not clobber the hoisted copy's. Test with the nested lockfile above and assert `deep` is in `bfs(['app-dep'], edges)`.

## Resolution
src/graph/index.ts npm branch keys edges by key.split('node_modules/').at(-1), matching parsers/npm.ts, and unions dependency lists when a name appears both hoisted and nested rather than clobbering. Two tests assert edges.get('nested') === ['deep'] and that the union case yields ['a','b'].
title: npm v2/v3 edge map keys nested packages by path, breaking --no-dev

## Problem

`parseYarnBerryLockfile` returns only `{ name, version }` (`yarn-berry.ts:29`) and types the parse result as `Record<string, Record<string, string>>` (`yarn-berry.ts:10`), which structurally cannot hold the nested `peerDependencies` / `dependencies` maps that Yarn Berry lockfiles do contain for every resolution.

## Evidence

A Yarn Berry `yarn.lock` entry looks like:

    "react-dom@npm:18.3.1":
      version: 18.3.1
      peerDependencies:
        react: ^18.3.1

`parseSyml` returns that nested map, and the parser drops it. The npm and pnpm parsers both propagate `peerDependencies` (`npm.ts:49`, `pnpm.ts:71`); berry is the odd one out. Compare `test/parsers/yarn-berry.test.ts`, which has a case named "parses package with engines field without error" — it asserts the parse does not throw, never that engines survive.

## Impact

On a Yarn Berry project the peer analysis — half the tool's stated purpose — depends entirely on the registry pass succeeding for every package. Under `--offline`, or on any registry miss (see the registry-failure finding), berry users get no peer constraints at all and a silently over-permissive range.

## Fix

Widen the parse type and propagate both fields:

    const parsed = parseSyml(content) as Record<string, {
      version?: string
      dependencies?: Record<string, string>
      peerDependencies?: Record<string, string>
    }>
    ...
    result.push({ name, version, peerDependencies: entry.peerDependencies })

Yarn Berry lockfiles do not record `engines`, so leave that to the registry pass. Extend the berry test to assert `peerDependencies` round-trips.

## Resolution
Introduced a YarnBerryEntry interface (version/dependencies/peerDependencies) replacing the too-narrow Record<string, Record<string,string>> cast, and parseYarnBerryLockfile now propagates entry.peerDependencies. Engines are still left to the registry pass - berry lockfiles do not record them. Test asserts react-dom's peerDependencies round-trip.
title: Yarn Berry parser discards peerDependencies present in the lockfile
Zero coverage on subsumption and OR-ranges — the module's two bug sites

body:
## Problem

`setVersionData` (`cache/index.ts:78`) and `setLatestData` (`cache/index.ts:111`) each call `save()` immediately after `setKey()`. `flat-cache.save()` serializes the _entire_ store and rewrites the file.

## Impact

A cold run over N packages performs up to 2N writes, and write k serializes k accumulated entries — O(N²) bytes written. For the 214-package example in the README that is ~428 rewrites of a growing JSON file; for a 2000-package monorepo lockfile it is ~4000 rewrites of a file that ends in the megabytes. The work is fsync-bound and lands on the user's real cache directory, so it also multiplies disk wear on every invocation. It is pure overhead: nothing reads the cache file mid-run, only the in-memory store.

## Evidence

`cache/index.ts:76-79` and `cache/index.ts:104-112` — `save()` is unconditional and inside the per-key setter. The only readers, `getVersionData`/`getLatestData`, go through `getKey()` against the in-memory store, never the file.

## Fix

Drop `save()` from both setters and flush once at process exit, after the render in `cli.ts`:

    // cache/index.ts
    export function flushCache(): void {
      versionsStore?.save()
      latestStore?.save()
    }

    // cli.ts, after console.log(output)
    flushCache()

Also call it from the `main().catch` handler (`cli.ts:187`) before `process.exit(1)` so a partial run still keeps what it fetched.

## Resolution
Removed save() from setVersionData and setLatestData; added flushCache() called once after render in cli.ts and again in the main().catch handler so a failed run still keeps what it fetched. Two tests cover persistence-after-flush and the no-op case.
title: Cache is fully serialized to disk on every single key write

body:
## Problem

`fetch(url)` at `client.ts:57` and `client.ts:90` is called with no `AbortSignal` and no timeout. Node's `fetch` has no default request timeout, so a connection that opens and then stalls — a hung corporate proxy, a black-holed route, a registry under load — leaves the promise pending indefinitely.

## Impact

`resolveRegistry` awaits each batch sequentially (`client.ts:164-170`), so one stalled request blocks the entire run. The ora spinner keeps animating, so the user sees a live-looking process that will never finish and never errors out; the only escape is Ctrl-C, which leaves the terminal cursor hidden (ora hides it on `start()` and only restores on `succeed`/`fail`).

## Evidence

`client.ts:55-68` and `client.ts:88-104` — the `try` blocks catch rejections but nothing ever produces one for a stalled socket. No `signal`, no `AbortSignal.timeout`, no agent-level timeout is configured anywhere in the repo.

## Fix

Node 24 has `AbortSignal.timeout`, and the repo targets `node24` (tsup.config.ts:6):

    const REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS) })

in both `fetchManifest` and `fetchLatest`. The existing `catch` already turns the resulting `TimeoutError` into `null`; combine with the registry-failure warning so timeouts are counted and surfaced rather than silently dropped.

## Resolution
Both fetch calls now pass signal: AbortSignal.timeout(REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS) with a 10s constant. Node 24 is the build target so AbortSignal.timeout is available. Timeouts surface through the existing catch, which now also increments the failure counter, so a stalled registry is both bounded and reported.
title: Registry fetches have no timeout; the CLI can hang forever

body:
## Problem

`computeIntersection` returns `{ intersection: null, conflicts: [] }` in two semantically opposite situations: when there is genuinely nothing to intersect, and when every input range failed `semver.validRange` (`intersect.ts:72-76`). `safeRangeText` cannot tell them apart — it branches only on `rangeCount === 0` (`table.ts:52`), and `rangeCount` is `target.ranges.length` (`table.ts:79`), which counts the _unfiltered_ entries.

## Evidence

Ran the real function:

    computeIntersection([{range:'garbage'}, {range:'also-bad'}])
    -> {"intersection":null,"conflicts":[]}

`target.ranges.length` is 2, so `safeRangeText(null, 2)` falls through to the final branch and renders `⚠  conflict — no safe range` (`table.ts:55`), while the "Conflicts at installed" section (`table.ts:105`) prints nothing because `conflicts` is empty. The user is told there is an irreconcilable conflict and shown zero packages causing it.

## Impact

Non-semver engine values are common in the wild (`"node": "current"`, `"npm": "please-use-yarn"`, git URLs in peer ranges). One such package turns a healthy report into a phantom conflict with no way to identify the culprit, which is worse than useless — it sends the user hunting a nonexistent problem.

## Fix

Distinguish the states in `IntersectionResult`:

    export interface IntersectionResult {
      intersection: string | null
      conflicts: RangeEntry[]
      invalid: RangeEntry[]     // ranges that failed semver.validRange
    }

populate `invalid` from the complement of the `valid` filter at `intersect.ts:72`, and in `safeRangeText` render `— (no parseable constraints)` when `conflicts.length === 0`. List the offending package names in a new section so they are actionable.

## Resolution
IntersectionResult gained an 'invalid' array; AnalysisTarget gained invalidRanges/latestInvalidRanges; safeRangeText now branches on conflictCount then invalidCount and renders '- (no parseable constraints)' instead of a phantom conflict. renderTarget lists the offending packages under 'Unparseable ranges'. Two renderer tests plus two analyzer tests cover it.
title: Unparseable ranges are rendered as a version conflict

## Problem

The README "Example output" block shows a layout the code cannot emit. Every structural element differs from `renderOutput`/`renderTarget` (src/output/table.ts:167, src/output/table.ts:65).

## Evidence

| README shows                                                      | Code emits                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `semver-ranger — package-lock.json (npm) — 214 packages analyzed` | `semver-ranger — analyzing 214 packages` then separate `Lockfile:` / `Targets:` rows (table.ts:182-192) |
| `node  (engines)  ·  6 packages declare a constraint`             | `node (engines)   6 package(s) declare a constraint` — no `·`, and `package(s)` (table.ts:69)           |
| Package table first, then `Safe range`                            | `Safe <name> range (installed):` and `(latest):` first, then the table (table.ts:77-97)                 |
| `Safe range (installed):`                                         | `Safe node range (installed):` — the target name is interpolated (table.ts:72)                          |
| —                                                                 | `Most restrictive (installed):` header above the table (table.ts:91), absent from the README            |

The README also never mentions the `Targets:` line or the second `--all` section, so a reader cannot predict the output they will get.

## Impact

The example is the page's main artifact — it is what a prospective user reads to decide whether the tool does what they need, and what a contributor diffs against when changing the renderer. It documents a format that has never existed in this codebase.

## Fix

Replace the block with real captured output:

    npm run build && node dist/cli.js --offline > /tmp/out.txt

and paste it verbatim. Add a test that renders a fixed `AnalysisTarget[]` through `renderOutput` and snapshot-compares, so the README block and the renderer cannot drift again silently.

## Resolution
Replaced the README example with output captured from the real renderer (generated by calling renderOutput directly on a representative package set), so all five structural mismatches are gone. Also fixed an adjacent inaccuracy found while verifying: README and CLAUDE.md claimed 'Node.js 22+' while package.json engines requires >=24.0.0.
title: README example output does not match what the renderer produces

body:
## Problem

`const REGISTRY = 'https://registry.npmjs.org'` (`client.ts:4`) is the only registry the client will ever contact. Nothing reads `.npmrc`, the `npm_config_registry` environment variable, per-scope registry mappings (`@acme:registry=...`), `_authToken`, or `HTTP(S)_PROXY`. `fetch` is called bare, with no proxy dispatcher.

## Impact

Three common environments degrade silently:

- **Private scopes.** `@acme/internal` is requested from registry.npmjs.org, which returns 404. `client.ts:58` maps that to `null` and the package contributes no constraints.
- **Registry mirrors / Artifactory / Verdaccio.** Organizations that block direct npmjs.org egress get a total resolution failure that renders as a clean table (see the registry-failure finding).
- **Corporate proxies.** Node's `fetch` does not honour `HTTPS_PROXY` without an explicit dispatcher, so every request fails.

In all three the tool exits 0 with an over-permissive range. Ironically, a lockfile-analysis tool that cannot read the lockfile's own registry configuration is most likely to be wrong exactly at the organizations that need it.

## Evidence

`grep -rn 'npmrc\|npm_config\|HTTPS_PROXY\|ProxyAgent\|dispatcher' src/` returns nothing. `client.ts:56` and `client.ts:89` interpolate the constant directly.

## Fix

Resolve the registry per package, honouring scope config:

    function registryFor(name: string): string {
      const scope = name.startsWith('@') ? name.slice(0, name.indexOf('/')) : null
      return process.env[`npm_config_${scope}:registry`]
        ?? process.env.npm_config_registry
        ?? 'https://registry.npmjs.org'
    }

When run via `npm exec`/`npx`, npm already exports the full `.npmrc` as `npm_config_*`, so this covers the common path with no new dependency and no `.npmrc` parser. For proxies, set a `ProxyAgent` dispatcher from `HTTPS_PROXY` when present. Document in the README that private registries need `npm exec semver-ranger` rather than a bare global invocation.

## Resolution
Added registryFor(name), which prefers npm_config_<scope>:registry, then npm_config_registry, then the public registry, and strips trailing slashes. npm exports the resolved .npmrc as npm_config_* under 'npm exec'/'npx', so private scopes and mirrors work with no .npmrc parser and no new dependency. Three tests cover default, override, and scope precedence. HTTPS_PROXY dispatcher support was NOT implemented - see the note in the run summary.
title: Registry URL hardcoded; .npmrc registry, proxy and auth ignored

body:
## Problem

The MegaLinter job checks out PR head with `token: ${{ secrets.PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (pr-lint.yml, "Checkout Code") and then runs `npm ci` ("Install dependencies") before any linting. `actions/checkout` defaults to `persist-credentials: true`, writing that token into `.git/config` as an `http.extraheader`. The job grants `contents: write`, `issues: write`, `pull-requests: write`, `security-events: write`.

`npm ci` executes `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` scripts from the PR's own `package.json` and lockfile. Both are attacker-controlled on a same-repository branch PR.

## Impact

A contributor with push access but not admin can add a `postinstall` that reads `.git/config` and exfiltrates the PAT — a personal access token whose scope is typically far broader than the repository. The job then goes on to `git-auto-commit-action` with `contents: write`, so the same script can also stage arbitrary content into the branch.

This is not reachable from forks: GitHub withholds secrets from `pull_request` runs originating in a fork, and the workflow additionally guards the commit steps with `head.repo.full_name == github.repository`. The exposure is to the same-repo-branch path, which the guards deliberately allow.

## Evidence

No `--ignore-scripts` anywhere in the workflows. `package.json` already carries an `allowScripts` allowlist (package.json:60-67), showing the project intends lifecycle scripts to be gated — the CI path bypasses that intent.

## Fix

Two independent mitigations, apply both:

    - name: Checkout Code
      uses: actions/checkout@...
      with:
        token: ${{ secrets.PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        persist-credentials: false
        fetch-depth: 0

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

`git-auto-commit-action` and `create-pull-request` both authenticate via their own `token` input, so `persist-credentials: false` does not break them. Apply `--ignore-scripts` to `ci.yml` and `publish.yml` too — neither needs dependency lifecycle scripts to lint, test, or run tsup.

## Resolution
npm ci --ignore-scripts in all three workflows (pr-lint, ci, publish), which closes the code-execution vector. ## Problem

The v1 branch of `parseNpmLockfile` returns `{name, version}` only (`npm.ts:57-60`) — correctly, since the v1 format records no `engines` or `peerDependencies`. All constraint data must therefore come from `resolveLocal` or the registry pass. Under `--offline` with no `node_modules` present, neither supplies anything.

## Impact

The run completes, prints `Parsed package-lock.json (N packages)`, and renders a table whose only content is `Targets: none` — indistinguishable from a project that genuinely declares no constraints. Nothing tells the user the combination of inputs they chose cannot produce an answer.

Also at `npm.ts:32`: `lock.lockfileVersion >= 2` is `false` when the field is absent or non-numeric, so a malformed or truncated lockfile silently takes the v1 path and yields `[]` rather than erroring.

## Evidence

`npm.ts:57-60` sets neither field. `client.ts:143-158` (offline branch) only spreads cache hits. `local.ts:35` returns the package untouched when no manifest is found. `test/fixtures/package-lock-v1.json` exercises the parse but no test covers the offline-with-no-node_modules combination.

## Fix

In `cli.ts`, after the analysis step, warn when the target list is empty but packages were parsed:

    if (allTargets.length === 0 && packages.length > 0) {
      console.error('Warning: no engine or peer constraints resolved. ' +
        'npm lockfileVersion 1 carries no metadata — run without --offline, or install node_modules.')
    }

Separately, make the version dispatch explicit and fail loudly on an unrecognised `lockfileVersion` rather than defaulting to the v1 shape.

## Resolution
cli.ts warns on stderr when packages were parsed but no analysis targets resolved, naming lockfileVersion 1 and pointing at --offline / node_modules as the cause. ## Problem

`registryFor()` resolves which registry to contact, but nothing configures how to reach it. `fetch` is called bare at `client.ts` in both `fetchManifest` and `fetchLatest`, and Node's `fetch` does not honour `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` without an explicit `ProxyAgent` dispatcher.

This is the residual of `audit-62ad8201`, which was resolved as fixed for the registry-URL and scope-authentication half. Splitting it out rather than leaving it inside a resolved finding, so the store does not report work as complete when part of it was not done.

## Evidence

`grep -rn 'ProxyAgent\|dispatcher\|HTTPS_PROXY' src/` returns nothing. The two `fetch` calls pass only `signal`.

## Impact

On a network that requires an egress proxy, every registry request fails. Behaviour is no longer silent — the failure counter added alongside the parent finding prints `Warning: N registry lookup(s) failed; the reported ranges may be too permissive` — so the run degrades loudly rather than lying. But the tool still cannot resolve anything in that environment, and `--offline` with a populated `node_modules` is the only workaround.

## Fix

Node ships `ProxyAgent` in undici; wire it when a proxy variable is present:

    import { ProxyAgent, setGlobalDispatcher } from 'undici'

    const proxy = process.env.HTTPS_PROXY ?? process.env.https_proxy
    if (typeof proxy === 'string' && proxy !== '') {
      setGlobalDispatcher(new ProxyAgent(proxy))
    }

`undici` is not currently a direct dependency, so this either adds one or waits for a stable global-agent API. Honour `NO_PROXY` before enabling it. Add a test that asserts the dispatcher is set when the variable is present.

## Resolution
Resolved by using Node's own proxy support rather than adding a dependency. Node 24 ships --use-env-proxy / NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, which routes global fetch through HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY and honours NO_PROXY. Verified experimentally that it cannot be enabled from inside a running process: setting process.env.NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY before the first fetch still resolved directly (ENOTFOUND against a proxy-only host), because Node reads it during bootstrap. Adding undici + EnvHttpProxyAgent was rejected: tsup bundles with noExternal so undici's wasm loader would be inlined into dist/cli.js, which is both large and fragile under esbuild. cli.ts now detects the case Node cannot fix for itself - a proxy variable set with proxy support off - and prints an actionable warning naming NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1, skipped under --offline. README documents it alongside private-registry configuration. Verified across four cases: proxy+off warns, proxy+on silent, no-proxy silent, --offline silent.
title: No proxy support: the registry client ignores HTTPS_PROXY

## Problem

`parseNpmLockfile` chooses its branch with `lock.lockfileVersion >= 2`. When the field is absent, a string, or otherwise non-numeric, the comparison is `false` and parsing silently falls through to the v1 shape, which reads `lock.dependencies` and returns `[]` for anything that is not a v1 lockfile.

This is the residual of `audit-23df4111`. That finding was resolved as fixed for the user-facing half — the CLI now warns when packages parsed but no constraints resolved — while the dispatch itself was explicitly left alone. Filed separately so the store does not carry an admission of unfinished work inside a resolved record.

## Evidence

`src/parsers/npm.ts`: `if (lock.lockfileVersion >= 2)`. A truncated or hand-edited `package-lock.json` with no `lockfileVersion` yields `[]` with no error. The CLI warning added for the parent finding fires only when zero targets resolve, so a malformed lockfile that still produces some registry hits stays invisible.

## Impact

A malformed lockfile is reported as a lockfile with no dependencies rather than as an error. Low severity because the common inputs are well-formed and the empty-analysis warning covers the total-failure case, but the parser should not guess.

## Fix

Dispatch explicitly and fail loudly on anything unrecognised:

    const version = lock.lockfileVersion
    if (typeof version !== 'number') {
      throw new Error('unrecognised package-lock.json: missing lockfileVersion')
    }
    if (version >= 2) { /* v2/v3 */ }
    if (version === 1) { /* v1 */ }
    throw new Error(`unsupported package-lock.json lockfileVersion: ${version}`)

`cli.ts` already surfaces thrown parse errors through the spinner's fail path. Add fixtures for a missing and an unknown `lockfileVersion`.

## Resolution
parseNpmLockfile now validates lockfileVersion instead of inferring it. A missing or non-numeric value threw the file into the v1 branch, which reads 'dependencies' and so returned [] for anything that was not a v1 lockfile - a malformed lockfile reported as one with no dependencies. The dispatch is explicit: non-numeric or non-finite throws 'expected a numeric lockfileVersion', >=2 takes the v2/v3 branch, ===1 the v1 branch, anything else throws naming the version. cli.ts already routes parse errors through the spinner's fail path to the top-level handler. Four tests cover missing, non-numeric, unsupported, and the still-working v1/v3 paths. All committed fixtures already declare the field, so no existing behaviour changed.
title: npm lockfileVersion dispatch does not validate the version

## Problem

ci.yml (job `CI`: lint, typecheck, test, build) and pr-lint.yml (job `MegaLinter`) are gate-shaped pull_request workflows, but main has no branch protection and its only ruleset has enforcement `disabled`, so neither check blocks a merge and main accepts direct pushes.

## Evidence

Tool: manual, Verified.

- `gh api repos/ivuorinen/semver-ranger/branches/main/protection` -> HTTP 404 "Branch not protected".
- `gh api repos/ivuorinen/semver-ranger/rulesets/2316946` -> name `main`, enforcement `disabled`, rules: deletion, non_fast_forward, required_linear_history, pull_request, update; no `required_status_checks` rule.

Re-verified 2026-09-13 after the ruleset was updated — still open:

- Ruleset 2316946 enforcement is now `active` with `required_status_checks: [{context: "ci / CI", integration_id: 15368}]`, strict policy on.
- `ci / CI` is the name ci.yml's job gets only when publish.yml calls it on a push to main (present in `gh api repos/ivuorinen/semver-ranger/commits/main/check-runs`). On pull requests the same job reports as `CI`: PR heads #123–#132 carry `CI` and zero `ci / CI` check runs. The required check can never be satisfied on a PR, so every PR is blocked for non-bypass actors (Renovate automerge stalls) while bypass actors merge past it.
- `MegaLinter` is not required.
- CodeQL default setup is `configured`, so the `code_scanning` rule has results to evaluate. Whether Code Quality is enabled for the `code_quality` rule is not exposed by `gh api repos/ivuorinen/semver-ranger` and is unverified.

## Impact

A PR with failing tests or lint merges to main and Publish.yml releases it; any contents:write token (e.g. pr-lint's) can push straight to main and trigger an npm release.

## Fix

In the `main` ruleset's `required_status_checks` rule, replace context `ci / CI` with `CI` and add `MegaLinter` (both GitHub Actions, integration 15368). Enforcement is already `active`. User-run (never auto-applied): edit at <https://github.com/ivuorinen/semver-ranger/rules/2316946>, then verify with `gh api repos/ivuorinen/semver-ranger/rulesets/2316946 --jq '.enforcement, [.rules[]|select(.type=="required_status_checks").parameters.required_status_checks[].context]'`.

User updated ruleset 2316946. Verified 2026-09-15: enforcement active; effective required_status_checks on main = CI and MegaLinter (integration 15368), strict policy on. Latest PR head reports check runs `CI` and `MegaLinter` from app 15368, so both contexts are satisfiable on pull requests. CodeQL default setup configured for the code_scanning rule; Code Quality enablement for the code_quality rule not exposed by the API and unverified.

## Problem

`key.replace(/\([^)]*\)/gu, '')` cannot strip nested parentheses. pnpm writes nested peer suffixes whenever a peer has its own peers, and the regex removes up to the first `)` only, leaving a stray `)` in the version.

## Evidence

src/parsers/pnpm.ts:26 and :67, and the same regex at src/graph/index.ts:66.

Reproduced: parsing a v9 lockfile with snapshot key `a@1.0.0(b@2.0.0(c@3.0.0))(d@4.0.0)` and a `packages` entry `a@1.0.0` declaring `engines: {node: '>=20'}` returns `{"name":"a","version":"1.0.0)"}` with no engines or peerDependencies.

## Fix

Cut at the first parenthesis instead of matching pairs: `const i = key.indexOf('('); const stripped = (i === -1 ? key : key.slice(0, i)).trim()`. Put it in one helper used by pnpm.ts and graph/index.ts, and add a nested-suffix fixture.

## Resolution
stripPeerSuffix cuts at the first parenthesis. Regression test covers a nested suffix; mutant restoring the old regex is killed.

## Problem

npm records an alias as `node_modules/<alias>` with the real package in `name`. The parser declares `name` (npm.ts:14) and never reads it, so the alias becomes the package name. Both Yarn parsers do the same with `alias@npm:real@range`. Registry lookups then query a different package, or one that does not exist.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `node_modules/string-width-cjs` with `name: string-width`, version 4.2.3 parses as `string-width-cjs@4.2.3`. The registry answers 404 for `/string-width-cjs/4.2.3` and 200 for `/string-width/4.2.3` (engines `>=8`). yarn-classic.ts and yarn-berry.ts both return `string-width-cjs@4.2.3`.

Live in this repository: `node_modules/@semantic-release/npm/node_modules/npm` has `name: ms`, yet the tool's `node` target contains the latest entry `npm@12.2.2` with range `^22.22.2 || ^24.15.0 || >=26.0.0`, which comes from a package the tree does not contain.

## Impact

An alias that exists on the registry injects an unrelated package's constraints into the intersection. One that does not exist produces a false "ranges may be too permissive" warning, and on Yarn lockfiles, which carry no engines, drops the constraint entirely.

## Fix

Use the real name for registry lookups (`entry.name ?? name`; parse `alias@npm:real@range` in both Yarn parsers). Keep the install path separately, because resolveLocal must still read `node_modules/<alias>/package.json`. Add alias fixtures for all three parsers.

## Resolution
npm v1, v2/v3 and both Yarn parsers now report the real name, and Package.alias keeps the install directory for resolveLocal and --no-dev. On this repo npm@12 no longer enters the latest range.
title: Aliased packages are analysed under the alias, pulling in the wrong package's data

body:
## Problem

registryFor reads `npm_config_@scope:registry` from the environment, and README.md:120-123 promises that `@acme:registry=` is picked up automatically under `npm exec`. npm never exports keys starting with `@`, so that variable cannot exist and every scoped package falls through to the mirror or public registry.

## Evidence

npm's `@npmcli/config/lib/set-envs.js:10`: `return !/^[/@_]/.test(key) &&`.

Reproduced with npm 11.19.1: `.npmrc` holding both `registry=` and `@acme:registry=` exports only `npm_config_registry` to `npm exec` and `npm run`. End to end under `npm exec` with two local servers, the mirror received `/@acme%2Fsecret/1.0.0` and `/@acme%2Fsecret/latest`; the scoped server received nothing.

## Impact

Internal package names are disclosed to whichever registry is the default, public npm included. If a public package has the same name, its manifest is used in the analysis. Users relying on the README's promise get no signal, and tests pass because they set the variable by hand.

## Fix

Resolve scope registries from `.npmrc` directly (project, then `~/.npmrc`), or from `npm config get @scope:registry` once per scope. Add a test driven by a real `.npmrc`, and correct README.md:120-123 to match what is then true.

## Resolution
readRegistries parses user and project .npmrc; README corrected. CLI test proves a scoped lookup reaches the scoped registry and nothing reaches the default. Global npmrc and ${VAR} expansion are out of scope and documented.
title: Per-scope registries are never honoured, so private package names reach the default registry

body:
## Problem

The repository has no contributor guide, while it enforces conventions a contributor can only discover by failing them. The `contributing` command rates an absent guide High when any enforced convention exists.

## Evidence

`find . -iname 'contributing*'` outside node_modules returns nothing. Enforced conventions: the `lint`, `typecheck`, `test` and `build` scripts in package.json; the `main` ruleset requires checks `CI` and `MegaLinter` and pull requests; releases come from Conventional Commits through semantic-release (.releaserc.json).

## Impact

A contributor is not told that commit types decide the release version, that CI runs `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, or which checks block a merge.

## Fix

Generate CONTRIBUTING.md from the real conventions: Node from .nvmrc, the five CI commands in order, the commit types and their release effect, the two required checks, and the review path from CODEOWNERS.

## Resolution
CONTRIBUTING.md written from the real scripts, commit rules and required checks; excluded from the npm tarball.
title: CONTRIBUTING.md is absent despite enforced build, test, commit and CI conventions

body:
## Problem

A key with no `node_modules/` segment, such as `packages/a`, survives `key.split('node_modules/').at(-1)` whole, so the directory path becomes the package name.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `{"packages/a": {"name": "@me/a", "version": "1.0.0", "engines": {"node": ">=22"}}}` parses as `{"name":"packages/a","version":"1.0.0",...}`. The registry answers 404 for `/packages/a/1.0.0`.

## Impact

Every workspace member costs two failed lookups, so each monorepo run prints a false "ranges may be too permissive" warning. Tables show paths instead of package names, and the warning stops meaning anything.

## Fix

Treat non-`node_modules/` keys as local: skip the registry for them and name them from `entry.name`. A workspace flag on Package keeps their own constraints in the analysis without a lookup.

## Resolution
Workspace members are named from entry.name or the directory basename, marked workspace, and skip registry lookups. Tests added.
title: npm workspace members are reported under their directory path

body:
## Problem

The v1 branch maps only the top level of `dependencies`. v1 nests non-hoisted versions under each entry's own `dependencies`, and those are never visited.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `{a: {version: '1.0.0', dependencies: {b: {version: '1.0.0'}}}, b: {version: '2.0.0'}}` returns only a@1.0.0 and b@2.0.0. The installed b@1.0.0 is missing. The docstring says versions 1, 2 and 3 are supported. buildEdgeMap's v1 branch (src/graph/index.ts:59-61) has the same flat walk.

## Impact

Older versions, the ones most likely to carry tight constraints, are absent from the analysis, so the safe range is too permissive with no warning.

## Fix

Walk `dependencies` recursively, deduplicating on name@version, in both the parser and the v1 edge map.

## Resolution
collectV1 and addV1Edges recurse into nested dependencies. Tests added.
title: npm v1 lockfiles lose every nested dependency

body:
## Problem

The npm branch unions edges for a name seen more than once, with a comment saying why. The pnpm (:73), yarn-classic (:81, :96) and yarn-berry (:102) branches overwrite instead, so only the last version's dependencies survive.

## Evidence

Reproduced with yarn-classic: prod `foo@^1` depends on `bar`, `foo@^2` has no deps, dev `devtool` depends on `bar` and `foo@^2`. filterDevPackages returns `['foo@1.0.0','foo@2.0.0']`: `bar` is gone although production needs it. buildEdgeMap returns `[["foo",[]]]` for the same shape on yarn-classic, yarn-berry and pnpm v6.

## Impact

A production package reachable only through an overwritten edge, and also used by a dev tool, is classed dev-only and removed, so its constraints vanish from the --no-dev result.

## Fix

Route all four branches through one `addEdges(name, deps)` helper that unions into a Set.

## Resolution
All formats route through addEdges, which unions. Tests cover yarn-classic, yarn-berry and pnpm, plus the production-package case.
title: Edge maps clobber earlier versions, so --no-dev can drop production packages

body:
## Problem

parsePnpmLockfile never checks `lockfileVersion`. v5 keys (`/pkg/1.0.0`, used through pnpm 7) do not match either pattern and are skipped, and scoped ones match wrongly. parseNpmLockfile rejects unknown versions precisely to avoid this.

## Evidence

Reproduced with `lockfileVersion: 5.4`: `/foo/1.0.0` disappears and `/@scope/bar/2.0.0_react@18.0.0` becomes `{"name":"@scope/bar/2.0.0_react","version":"18.0.0"}`, with exit 0. An empty file throws `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'packages')`.

## Impact

A v5 lockfile is analysed as though it had almost no packages, and reports a clean, confident, wrong result.

## Fix

Validate the root is a mapping and `lockfileVersion` is at least 6, throwing the same style of error as the npm parser; or add v5 key parsing if v5 is meant to be supported.

## Resolution
readLock rejects a non-mapping root and lockfileVersion below 6, as the npm parser does; README states the supported range.
title: Unsupported pnpm lockfile versions silently lose or garble packages

body:
## Problem

Range collectors only exclude `undefined` and `'*'`, so a number or null is recorded as a range. It is classified invalid, then the table renderer calls `.trim()` on it.

## Evidence

Reproduced: a lockfile entry with `engines: {node: 18}` exits 1 with `Error: text.trim is not a function`; with `{node: null}`, `Error: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'trim')`. The call is src/output/table.ts:27. src/analyzer/peers.ts:65-70 has the same check. The value can come from registry manifests, which are cast, not validated.

## Impact

One malformed manifest anywhere in the tree discards the entire run, after every lookup has already been paid for, and the message names neither the package nor the field.

## Fix

Accept only strings: `if (typeof range === 'string' && range !== '*')` in the three collectors. Report a non-string value through invalidRanges as `String(value)` so it stays visible.

## Resolution
rangeText prefixes non-string values so they land in invalidRanges and render as unparseable. Verified end to end.
title: A non-string engines or peer value aborts the whole analysis

body:
## Problem

WIDTH is taken from `process.stdout.columns` whenever it is defined, including 0. `'─'.repeat(WIDTH - 4)` at table.ts:141 then throws.

## Evidence

Reproduced on a real pseudo-terminal with a 0x0 window, which is what a pty allocated without a size reports: exit 1, `Error: Invalid count value: -4`. The parse and local phases had already succeeded.

## Impact

The analysis completes and is then thrown away, with an error that says nothing useful, in environments such as `ssh -tt` from a script.

## Fix

`const WIDTH = process.stdout.columns || 80` handles 0 and undefined; clamp with `Math.max(WIDTH - 4, 0)` for very narrow terminals.

## Resolution
WIDTH falls back on 0 as well as undefined, and the rule length is clamped. Verified on a real 0x0 pty; test asserts the 80-column layout.
title: A terminal reporting zero columns crashes rendering

body:
## Problem

The per-request timeout exists, but batches run one after another and nothing stops after repeated timeouts, so total time scales with package count.

## Evidence

Reproduced against a local server that accepts connections and never answers: 8 packages took 20.1 s and reported 16 failed lookups. That is 10 s per batch of 4, so a 2,000-package lockfile would take about 83 minutes.

## Impact

On a filtered network, the case warnIfProxyIgnored exists for, the CLI sits behind a spinner for over an hour and a CI job burns its whole timeout, then reports a result built from nothing.

## Fix

Stop after two consecutive batches in which every request failed by timeout, treat the rest as unresolved, and warn that the remaining lookups were skipped and --offline is available.

## Resolution
Stops after two batches in which every request timed out and reports the skipped count. 40 packages against a stalled server went from 100 s to 20.1 s.
title: A stalled registry costs 10 seconds per batch with no circuit breaker

body:
## Problem

Offline resolution always returns `failed: 0`. A package with no cache entry and no matching node_modules manifest contributes nothing and nothing is reported. src/cli.ts:217-218 states the opposite rule: a dropped constraint must never be silent.

## Evidence

Reproduced: a yarn.lock with a and b, only a installed (engines `>=10`). `--offline --json` exits 0, reports intersection `>=10.0.0` from 1 range, and stderr is empty. The existing warning fires only when no target resolves at all.

## Impact

Yarn classic and npm v1 lockfiles carry no metadata, so any partially installed project gets a range that looks authoritative but ignores the unresolved packages.

## Fix

Count packages for which neither the lockfile, a matching local manifest, nor the cache supplied metadata, return it as `failed`, and print the same "may be too permissive" warning.

## Resolution
Package.hasMetadata marks packages with known constraints; resolveOffline reports the rest and the CLI warns, naming them.
title: --offline silently widens the range when packages have no metadata

body:
## Problem

A missing or malformed package.json makes filterDevPackages return every package with no signal. The user asked for a filter and gets an unfiltered result labelled as if it were filtered.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `package.json` containing `{ not json` and a dev-only package with engines `>=20`. `--offline --no-dev --json` exits 0, still counts the dev package, and stderr is empty. src/analyzer/peers.ts:44-46 has the same silent catch for peer detection.

## Impact

An explicit flag fails open: dev constraints stay in a result the user believes is production-only.

## Fix

Throw from filterDevPackages so the run exits 1 naming the file, since the requested filter cannot be applied. In detectPeerTargets, warn on a parse failure and stay silent only for a missing file.

## Resolution
--no-dev now exits 1 without a usable package.json; an unparseable file otherwise warns that peer detection was skipped. CLI tests added.
title: --no-dev silently does nothing when package.json is unreadable

body:
## Problem

openStore guards only against unparseable JSON. Entries are never validated, so valid JSON with the wrong shape reaches `entry.cachedAt`. The openStore docstring says a corrupt cache must never fail a run.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `latest.json` containing `{"foo":null}` with a lockfile that has `foo` exits 1 with `Error: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'cachedAt')`. An entry without `cachedAt` gives `NaN > TTL`, which is false, so it never expires.

## Impact

A leftover file from another format version, or a partial edit, breaks the CLI until the user finds and deletes a cache file whose location is not documented.

## Fix

In getLatestData, treat an entry as missing unless `typeof entry?.cachedAt === 'number' && typeof entry.data?.version === 'string'`; in openStore, also require the root to be a plain object.

## Resolution
isFresh validates entry shape, and openStore requires an object root. test/cache/limits.test.ts covers null, partial and non-object data.
title: A well-formed cache file of the wrong shape fails the run

body:
## Problem

andRanges distributes AND across OR-groups and keeps every satisfiable pair without simplifying or deduplicating. Overlapping groups all survive, so the combined range doubles with each package.

## Evidence

Measured with n packages declaring `>=4 || >=6`: n=14 109 ms, n=16 461 ms, n=18 1,236 ms, n=20 5,237 ms, n=21 10,939 ms. Disjoint ranges stay fast (2,000 entries in 61 ms), so only overlap triggers it.

## Impact

About 30 packages sharing one overlapping range, such as a family published from a monorepo, make the run effectively never finish. The range text comes from third-party manifests, so dependency metadata can hang the tool.

## Fix

In andRanges, simplify each group with simplifyGroup and deduplicate through a Set before joining. simplifyGroup already exists and reduces these groups to two.

## Resolution
andRanges simplifies each group and deduplicates. 40 overlapping entries finish instantly under a 5 s test timeout.
title: Overlapping OR-groups grow exponentially during intersection

body:
## Problem

buildEdgeMap re-parses all four formats with its own patterns, independent of src/parsers. This breaks the single-parser rule in docs/audit/arch-profile.md, and the two copies have diverged.

## Evidence

The pnpm key regexes are duplicated at src/parsers/pnpm.ts:29,35 and src/graph/index.ts:68-69, and the suffix strip at pnpm.ts:26 and graph/index.ts:66. The Yarn Berry protocol lists differ: yarn-berry.ts:42 omits `workspace`, graph/index.ts:100 includes it. The earlier resolved finding audit-2755c66e fixed peer-suffix handling on one side only.

## Impact

A format fix has to be found and made twice, which is how the pnpm v9 and clobbered-edge defects exist alongside a correct-looking parser.

## Fix

Have each parser return its packages and edges together from one walk of the lockfile, and reduce src/graph to the reachability logic.

## Resolution
Each parser module now owns its format's packages and edges through shared key helpers; src/graph holds only dispatch and reachability. Two functions per module rather than one combined walk, which kept the parser API and its tests intact.
title: Every lockfile format is parsed twice by separate code

body:
## Problem

No test imports or spawns the CLI. `node --experimental-test-coverage` lists only files that were loaded, so the 99.76% figure excludes the 261-line entry point that wires everything together.

## Evidence

`grep -rl 'cli.ts\|cli.js' test` returns nothing, and cli.ts is absent from the coverage table. Mutants that survived the full suite: `process.exit(1)` to `process.exit(0)`, `if (failedLookups > 0)` to `if (false)`, `if (values['no-dev'] === true)` to `if (false)`.

## Impact

The documented exit-code contract, the too-permissive warning, and --no-dev itself can all be removed with CI green.

## Fix

Add one spawn-based test file covering exit 0 and exit 1, --json, --no-dev, --offline and the failed-lookup warning, using a local server through `npm_config_registry`.

## Resolution
test/cli.test.ts spawns the CLI for exit codes, flags, --no-dev, --offline, warnings and registry selection. The three surviving cli.ts mutants are now killed.
title: src/cli.ts has no tests and sits outside the coverage report

body:
## Problem

Line coverage is near 100% but several behaviours are executed without being asserted. Fixtures also miss the real-world shapes behind this audit's parser defects.

## Evidence

Of 29 single-line mutants, 13 survived, 3 of them in cli.ts. Survivors include: reversing the `<` sort in simplifyGroup so the widest upper bound wins; swapping registry-over-lockfile precedence (client.ts:171); removing the request timeout (client.ts:95); dropping the root-entry skip in npm.ts:50, because fixture roots have no version; `name in allDeps` replaced by `true` (peers.ts:40). test/fixtures/pnpm-lock-v9.yaml has 16 lines and no nested peer suffix.

## Impact

The upper-bound survivor means the tool's central output could report a wider range than is safe with every test passing.

## Fix

Add asserting tests for each survivor: a two-upper-bound intersection, precedence when both sources declare engines, a request that never completes, a root entry with a version, and peer detection excluding undeclared packages.

## Resolution
Asserting tests added for each named survivor. Re-run: 45 of 46 mutants killed once the weak zero-columns test was tightened; the survivor only appends a space, which is equivalent behaviour.
title: Mutations to core logic survive the test suite

body:
## Problem

Finding class: supply-chain. `.npmrc` sets no `min-release-age`, so a manual `npm install` or `npm update` can resolve a version published minutes ago.

## Evidence

opengrep `npm-missing-minimum-release-age` at .npmrc:1, severity MEDIUM. `npm config ls -l` shows `min-release-age = null`, and npm 11.19.1 defines the option. Renovate's `renovate/stability-days` check covers bot pull requests only.

## Impact

A human dependency change has no cooldown against a freshly compromised release, the window in which most malicious versions are caught and pulled.

## Fix

Add `min-release-age=7` to .npmrc, matched to the Renovate stability window.

## Resolution
.npmrc sets min-release-age=7, excluding @ivuorinen/* which Renovate updates immediately, and renovate.json matches at 7 days. opengrep reports 0; npm ci and a lockfile re-resolve under the window are unchanged.
title: No minimum release age for packages installed outside Renovate

body:
## Problem

Class: excess-permissions. The job persists `secrets.PAT || GITHUB_TOKEN` in .git/config. The comment at :43-46 relies on `npm ci --ignore-scripts` to keep it safe, but that only stops lifecycle scripts. MegaLinter's Prettier loads `.prettierrc.mjs`, which imports a package from the node_modules that the PR installed.

## Evidence

.prettierrc.mjs:1 `import config from '@ivuorinen/prettier-config'`. Run 36400500181, on a Renovate PR, logged `Command: [prettier --write package-lock.json package.json]` with `Rules config: identified by [prettier]`. Fork PRs do not get the PAT; same-repository PRs, including Renovate's, do. Gating is verified: the `main` ruleset requires `CI` and `MegaLinter`.

## Impact

Scenario: a Renovate PR bumps a compromised version of that config package or anything it imports. Prettier executes it during the lint step, and it reads the PAT from .git/config, gaining repository write outside the workflow's permission block.

## Fix

Check out with `persist-credentials: false`, and add the credential only for the final push step, after MegaLinter has exited. Otherwise stop auto-committing fixes (`APPLY_FIXES: none`), which removes the need for a write credential here at all. Correct the comment at :43-46 either way.

## Resolution
Checkout uses persist-credentials: false; a new step adds the push credential only after MegaLinter has exited. actionlint and zizmor are clean. Not exercised in a real workflow run.
title: Dependency code loaded by MegaLinter's Prettier runs beside a persisted write token

Class: excess-permissions. The comment says SARIF_REPORTER uploads to code scanning. The reporter only writes a file into megalinter-reports, and the workflow has no upload-sarif step.

`security-events: write # SARIF_REPORTER uploads results to code scanning` at :30. The only step handling reports is upload-artifact at :84-90. No `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` appears in any workflow.

A write scope with no user sits on the job that runs the most third-party code.

Removed security-events: write from the MegaLinter job.

body:
## Problem

Only ci.yml sets `timeout-minutes`. The publish job and the MegaLinter job (pr-lint.yml:21-23) fall back to the 360-minute default.

## Evidence

`timeout-minutes` appears once in .github/workflows, at ci.yml:21. publish.yml declares `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress: false`.

## Impact

A hung release holds an OIDC-capable, write-scoped job for six hours, and later releases queue behind it because nothing cancels the run.

Add `timeout-minutes: 20` to the publish job and `timeout-minutes: 30` to the MegaLinter job.

Added timeout-minutes: 20 to publish and 30 to MegaLinter.

body:
## Problem

package.json declares `engines.node: >=24.0.0`, while CI runs only the `.nvmrc` version, 26.10.0. A change that needs Node 26 passes every gate and ships to Node 24 users.

## Evidence

ci.yml uses `node-version-file: '.nvmrc'` and has no matrix. All 161 tests pass today on Node 24.14.1 when run by hand, so this is a missing gate, not a current failure.

## Impact

The engines field is a published promise that nothing checks, in a tool whose purpose is analysing engines constraints.

## Fix

Add a second job that runs `npm test` on Node 24. Keep the existing `CI` job as it is, because a matrix would rename the required status check.

## Resolution
New node-floor job runs npm test on Node 24, separate from the required CI job so its check name is unchanged. All 230 tests pass on 24.14.1 locally.
title: CI never tests the declared Node floor

body:
## Problem

zizmor's `self-repository` audit prefers `$/...` over `./...` for a same-repository `uses:`.

## Evidence

zizmor 1.31.1 `--pedantic`: `help[self-repository]` at publish.yml:18, `uses: ./.github/workflows/ci.yml`, severity Low, confidence High. It is the only unsuppressed result. actionlint and checkov report none. No exploit path exists; the reference already resolves within the repository.

## Impact

None today; this keeps pedantic zizmor runs clean.

## Fix

Change the line to `uses: $/.github/workflows/ci.yml` once actionlint accepts that syntax, or add `# zizmor: ignore[self-repository]`.

## Resolution
Added an inline zizmor ignore, the alternative named in the finding, rather than changing the uses: path on the release workflow.
title: zizmor pedantic: reusable workflow uses ./ rather than the self-repository syntax

body:
## Problem

Finding class: sast. encodeName replaces only the first `/` and the version is not encoded at all, so a crafted lockfile can change the request path.

## Evidence

CodeQL `js/incomplete-sanitization` at client.ts:70: `name.replace('/', '%2F')`, normalized to High because the SARIF result carries no level. src/registry/client.ts:94 interpolates `version` raw. CodeQL's planted control `js/command-line-injection` fired, so the run was live.

Severity set to Low on review: the host is fixed by configuration, requests are unauthenticated GETs, and valid npm names hold one slash.

## Impact

A malicious lockfile can make the CLI issue GET requests to other paths on the configured registry. It cannot change the host, attach credentials, or write anything.

## Fix

`encodeURIComponent(name).replace(/^%40/u, '@')` for the name and `encodeURIComponent(version)` for the version.

## Resolution
Name and version are fully URL-encoded, keeping only the scope's leading @. The CodeQL alert no longer fires; its planted control still does.
title: Lockfile-controlled name and version enter registry URLs unencoded

body:
## Problem

Package names, versions and ranges are printed as received. An invalid range is displayed verbatim in the Unparseable section, so a manifest controls bytes written to the terminal.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `engines: {node: "\u001b]0;pwned\u0007nope"}` exits 0 and stdout contains the raw ESC sequence.

## Impact

A malicious package can overwrite earlier lines, for example a conflict warning, or send OSC sequences that some terminals act on, against a user who only analysed a lockfile.

## Fix

In `wrap`, strip C0 and C1 control characters before measuring: `text.replace(/[\u0000-\u001F\u007F-\u009F]/gu, '')`. `--json` is already safe because JSON.stringify escapes them.

## Resolution
wrap() strips control characters. Verified: no raw ESC in stdout.
title: Registry and lockfile text reaches the terminal with escape sequences intact

body:
## Problem

The seed entry is accepted without a satisfiability check. When nothing else conflicts with it, its range is returned as the intersection.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `computeIntersection([{range: '>=18 <16'}])` returns `{"intersection":">=18.0.0 <16.0.0-0","conflicts":[]}`.

## Impact

The output presents an empty range as "Safe node range" where a conflict should be reported.

## Fix

Before returning the intersection, check `semver.minVersion(best.combined) === null`, and in that case return null with the entry listed in conflicts.

## Resolution
A lone unsatisfiable range now returns a conflict. Test added.
title: A single unsatisfiable range is reported as the safe range

body:
## Problem

Latest data is per package name, but it is collected once per installed version, so one package casts several votes in the largest-agreeing-set search. src/analyzer/peers.ts:69-76 does the same.

## Evidence

Reproduced with a@1.0.0, a@2.0.0 and b@1.0.0: `latestRanges` is `['a@3.0.0','a@3.0.0','b@3.0.0']`.

## Impact

Tables show duplicate rows, and "N package(s) block upgrade" can name the wrong side when a package with many installed copies outvotes several distinct packages.

## Fix

Deduplicate on package name in collectLatestRanges and the peers loop.

## Resolution
analyzeTarget collects latest data once per package name. Test added.
title: Multiple installed versions inflate the latest-version analysis

body:
## Problem

The section heading promises the most restrictive constraints, but the loop prints every entry in `target.ranges`, unsorted and unfiltered.

## Evidence

table.ts:173 `ui.div('  Most restrictive (installed):')`, followed by `for (const entry of target.ranges)` at :181 with no sort or filter. The README example output shows the same unordered list.

## Impact

On a real tree the section is hundreds of rows, and a reader will take the top rows to be the constraints that matter.

## Fix

Either sort by `semver.minVersion` descending and show those that set the bound, or rename the heading to "Declared constraints (installed)".

## Resolution
Heading renamed to "Declared constraints (installed)" in the renderer and README.
title: "Most restrictive" lists every package in lockfile order

body:
## Problem

`--all` is documented as showing packages with no constraints, but JSON mode returns before showAll is read. Nothing warns that the flag was ignored.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `--offline --json` and `--offline --json --all` produce byte-identical stdout. The README option table states no such limitation.

## Impact

A script asking for every package silently gets a partial list.

## Fix

Emit `{ targets, packages }` under --all, which is a JSON shape change to flag in the release; or document that --all applies to table output only.

## Resolution
Documented --all as table-only in --help and README, leaving the JSON shape unchanged.
title: --all has no effect on --json output

body:
## Problem

The warning always says npm lockfileVersion 1 carries no metadata and suggests running without --offline, whatever the actual lockfile and mode.

## Evidence

Reproduced on an online run against a v3 lockfile with a stalled registry: stderr prints `npm lockfileVersion 1 carries no metadata — run without --offline`. The check is only `allTargets.length === 0 && packages.length > 0`.

## Impact

It sends users after a cause that does not apply, directly after a registry failure that actually explains the result.

## Fix

Say only what is known: "no engine or peer constraints were resolved", and suggest `--offline` or `node_modules` according to the mode that ran.

## Resolution
Warning no longer names npm v1, and suggests remedies only under --offline. CLI test added.
title: The empty-analysis warning blames npm v1 for every lockfile type

body:
## Problem

parseArgs runs at module top level, outside main's error handler, so usage errors surface as an uncaught exception.

## Evidence

Reproduced: `semver-ranger --bogus` exits 1 with 18 lines of stderr beginning `node:internal/util/parse_args/parse_args:102`.

## Impact

## Problem

Writes go to a per-process temporary file and are renamed into place. Last writer still wins, as documented in flushCache.

## Problem

`readLock` parses the whole file with `parseYaml(content)` (pnpm.ts:46), which accepts exactly one YAML document. pnpm 12 writes two documents whenever package.json has a `packageManager` field: first an env document (`---`, `packageManagerDependencies`), then the lockfile itself. pnpm 11 does the same once config dependencies exist (`pnpm add --config`). ## Evidence

Reproduced with pnpm 12.6.0 in a project whose package.json is `{"name":"pm","version":"1.0.0","packageManager":"pnpm@12.6.0","dependencies":{"ms":"2.1.3"}}`. After `pnpm install`, pnpm-lock.yaml contains 2 `---` separators. `node src/cli.ts --offline` exits 1 with `Error: Source contains multiple documents; please use YAML.parseAllDocuments() at line 158, column 1`. Script: the repro-pnpm.sh P1 section the parser reviewer wrote. No test fixture contains a multi-document pnpm lockfile.

Every pnpm 12 project that pins its package manager, which is the standard corepack setup, cannot be analysed at all. The tool fails before printing anything.

## Fix

In `readLock`, parse with `parseAllDocuments(content)`. Take the last document, which is the lockfile proper; the env document always comes first. Throw that document's `errors[0]` if it has one, and convert it with `.toJS()`. Do not analyse the env document: package-manager and config dependencies are not project dependencies. Add a two-document fixture written by pnpm 12, with tests for both the parser and `pnpmInstallSets`.

## Resolution
readLock (src/parsers/pnpm.ts) now uses parseAllDocuments, throws the first document error, and reads the last document, so the env document pnpm 11+ writes first is ignored. Tests: parsePnpmLockfile env document, rejects malformed YAML, and filterDevPackages on a two-document pnpm lockfile. The real pnpm 12.6.0 two-document lockfile from the review repro now exits 0. npm run cov 377/377 at 100%.

## Problem

Finding class: supply-chain. The publish job (permissions `contents: write`, `id-token: write # OIDC for npm trusted publishing`) runs `cycjimmy/semantic-release-action@ad51787… # v8.1.4` with no `with:` block. At that SHA the action always runs `installSpecifyingVersionSemantic`, which executes `npm install semantic-release${versionSuffix}` in the action's own directory, and the suffix is empty when `semantic_version` is unset (action.yml: "If no version range is specified, latest version will be used by default"). That install has no lockfile, so semantic-release and its whole dependency tree resolve fresh on every release.

## Evidence

Verified via `gh api repos/cycjimmy/semantic-release-action/contents/...?ref=ad51787758d9654d5a75150a89a6fa9b3ccef95e`: src/index.js calls `installSpecifyingVersionSemantic()` unconditionally; src/installSpecifyingVersionSemantic.task.js runs `['install', \`semantic-release${versionSuffix}\`, ...]` with `cwd: path.resolve(__dirname, '..')`. `npm view semantic-release` today: latest 26.0.1, published 2026-11-16T04:22Z (26.0.0 one hour earlier); package-lock.json locks 25.0.9. The repo .npmrc `min-release-age=7` does not apply to an install in the action's directory, and `.github/scripts/release-notes-smoke.mjs` exercises only the locked plugins.

## Impact

The next merge to main runs a one-day-old semantic-release major, plus whatever its unlocked dependencies resolve to, inside the job that can publish @ivuorinen/semver-ranger to npm and push tags. A compromised or breaking release of any package in that tree runs with publish rights, bypassing the SHA pinning, integrity hashes and 7-day cooldown the rest of the pipeline relies on; a breaking major can also simply fail the release.

## Fix

Run the locked binary instead of the action: replace the step with `- run: npm exec --no -- semantic-release` and `env: GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (node_modules/.bin/semantic-release is 25.0.9 with an integrity hash, installed by the existing `npm ci --ignore-scripts`). If the action stays, at minimum pin `with: semantic_version: 25.0.9`, accepting that its transitive tree remains unlocked.

## Resolution
publish.yml replaces cycjimmy/semantic-release-action with `run: npm exec --no -- semantic-release`. That runs the locked semantic-release 25.0.9 from npm ci (node_modules/.bin), with the same GITHUB_TOKEN env and a comment saying why. actionlint and zizmor --pedantic are clean. CLAUDE.md now lists semantic-release among the tools hoisted from config packages.
title: Publish job installs an unpinned semantic-release at release time with OIDC publish rights

CLAUDE.md:20,47,49. `ls .claude` → no such directory; np_check_rules_anatomy: "no rules directory". The installed context-mode block's rules (lines 54-124) were excluded from the count as installed text.

Path-scoped or atomic rules cannot be loaded selectively or audited per file, and the mandates are easy to miss inside architecture prose.

Create `.claude/rules/node-version-nvm.md` (unconditional: use the .nvmrc version via nvm), `.claude/rules/runtime-dependencies.md` (use Node built-ins; add a runtime dependency beyond semver/yaml only with approval — the unhedged wording tightens the rule, so confirm it with the owner) and `.claude/rules/config-package-tools.md` (the devDependencies procedure), then remove each line from CLAUDE.md once its file exists.
