body:
## Problem

The fix for ci-88c2b570 removed the persisted checkout credential ("No credential while the linters run: Prettier imports code from the node_modules this PR installed", line 41), but the MegaLinter step still receives `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (line 77). MegaLinter is a Docker action (`runs: using: docker`), so step env reaches the container, where Prettier loads `.prettierrc.mjs` → `@ivuorinen/prettier-config` from the PR's node_modules. The job token carries `contents: write`, `issues: write`, `pull-requests: write`, `statuses: write`. Second vector: that code can also plant `.git/hooks/pre-commit`/`pre-push` in the writable workspace; the later steps put the push token into `.git/config` (line 128) and git-auto-commit-action (line 136) runs `git commit`/`push` without `--no-verify`.

## Evidence

pr-lint.yml:26-35 job permissions; :41-44 checkout comment and `persist-credentials: false`; :68 `uses: oxsecurity/megalinter@f2fe8c1… # v10.2.0`; :77 `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`; :121 `sudo chown -Rc $UID .git/`; :127-128 token written into the remote URL; :136 git-auto-commit-action with no commit_options. megalinter action.yml at that SHA: `using: "docker"`. .prettierrc.mjs line 1: `import config from '@ivuorinen/prettier-config'`. Same-repo PRs only (fork PRs get a read-only token); Renovate opens same-repo PRs.

## Impact

A compromised dependency arriving in a Renovate PR (or a malicious collaborator branch) runs during lint with a token that can push to branches, edit PRs/issues and forge commit statuses — the exact exposure ci-88c2b570 was meant to close, and the workflow comment says it is closed.

## Fix

Never run PR code in a job holding a write token: split into a `megalinter` job with `permissions: contents: read`, no GITHUB_TOKEN env (set `GITHUB_STATUS_REPORTER: false` in .mega-linter.yml, the job result is the status) that uploads `git diff --binary` as an artifact, and a `push-fixes` job (`needs: megalinter`, same-repo PRs only) that checks out the head ref fresh, `git apply`s the artifact and pushes with `git commit --no-verify`. Alternatively set `APPLY_FIXES: none` and drop the write permissions and the push steps. Correct the line-41 comment either way.

## Resolution
The owner chose the alternative fix. pr-lint.yml: job permissions are contents: read and packages: read; there is no GITHUB_TOKEN in the MegaLinter env, the APPLY_FIXES env is gone, and all five fix/commit/push steps are deleted. The checkout comment now says nothing pushes, and the job name stays MegaLinter for the required check. .mega-linter.yml: APPLY_FIXES: none, GITHUB_COMMENT_REPORTER and GITHUB_STATUS_REPORTER are false, so the job result is the check. The .gitignore comment was updated to match. actionlint is clean, zizmor --pedantic reports no findings, and .mega-linter.yml validates against the v10.2.0 schema.
title: PR-installed dependency code runs in MegaLinter with the write-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment

body:
## Problem

The push uses `PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`, and no `PAT` secret exists, so the fix commit is pushed with GITHUB_TOKEN. GitHub does not start workflow runs for pushes made with GITHUB_TOKEN, so the new head SHA never gets `CI` or `MegaLinter` results; with strict required checks the PR stays blocked until someone pushes again by hand.

## Evidence

`gh secret list` returns nothing. pr-lint.yml:127 `PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PAT || secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`. Ruleset: required checks ["CI","MegaLinter"], strict_required_status_checks_policy true.

## Impact

Every PR that MegaLinter auto-fixes ends up with a head commit that has no required checks, silently stalling the merge.

## Fix

Create the `PAT` secret the workflow already references (a fine-grained token or GitHub App token limited to contents write on this repo), or, if auto-fix commits are rare, document in CONTRIBUTING.md "after a MegaLinter fix commit, push an empty commit to re-run checks". If ci-fef57f3e (the MegaLinter token finding) is fixed by dropping APPLY_FIXES, this finding goes with it.

## Resolution
Resolved with ci-fef57f3e, as this finding anticipated: pr-lint.yml no longer commits or pushes MegaLinter fixes, and has no PAT or GITHUB_TOKEN references, so no un-checked fix commits can appear. CONTRIBUTING.md tells contributors to run npm run lint:fix themselves.
title: MegaLinter fix commits pushed with GITHUB_TOKEN never trigger the required checks

body:
## Problem

Config drift. The new top-level `"minimumReleaseAge": "7 days"` is overridden for every npm dependency: the extended `github>ivuorinen/renovate-config` includes `security:minimumReleaseAgeNpm`, whose preset adds the packageRule `{matchDatasources: ["npm"], minimumReleaseAge: "3 days"}` (and passes 3 days to npm as `minimumReleaseAgePackageManager`). packageRules apply after top-level config, so npm updates use 3 days. `.npmrc:4-5` states the opposite: "Skip versions published in the last 7 days, the window .github/renovate.json also waits."

## Evidence

ivuorinen/renovate-config default.json `extends` includes `security:minimumReleaseAgeNpm`; renovatebot/renovate lib/config/presets/internal/security.preset.ts `buildMinimumReleaseAgePreset` returns `packageRules: [{ internalChecksFilter: 'strict', matchDatasources: [datasource], minimumReleaseAge }]` with npm `minimumReleaseAge: '3 days'`. .github/renovate.json has no packageRules.

## Impact

The documented 7-day supply-chain cooldown is 3 days for Renovate's npm updates: either Renovate raises PRs whose lockfile update npm refuses until day 7 (red PRs), or the package-manager age it passes lets 3-day-old versions into the lockfile. Either way the policy the .npmrc comment describes does not hold.

## Fix

Add to .github/renovate.json: `"packageRules": [{ "matchDatasources": ["npm"], "matchPackageNames": ["!@ivuorinen/**"], "minimumReleaseAge": "7 days" }]` (the exclusion keeps the shared config's immediate own-package updates), and set `"npm": { "minimumReleaseAgePackageManager": "7 days" }` so the age passed to npm matches .npmrc.

## Resolution
.github/renovate.json adds a packageRule: npm datasource, !@ivuorinen/**, update types major/minor/patch, minimumReleaseAge 7 days, with a description saying why. matchUpdateTypes keeps the preset's age waivers for lockFileMaintenance, pin and other types with no release timestamp. npm.minimumReleaseAgePackageManager was not added: it only applies with minimumReleaseAgePackageManagerSync, and .npmrc's min-release-age already makes npm enforce 7 days. Option names were checked against renovate-schema.json 44.259.0. renovate-config-validator 44.249.1 --strict passes.
title: Renovate's 7-day release age does not apply to npm packages, contradicting .npmrc

body:
## Problem

`readLock` calls `parseYaml(content)` with the default `uniqueKeys: true`. For every key, yaml 2.9.1's duplicate-key check scans the mapping's existing pairs (`mapIncludes` → `items.some(...)`), so parsing is O(n²) in the number of `packages` and `snapshots` keys. `readLock` runs twice under `--no-dev`: from `parsePnpmLockfile` (:97) and again from `pnpmInstallSets` (:157). The Yarn Berry parser already passes `uniqueKeys: false` (yarn-berry.ts:35).

## Evidence

Measured with `performance.now()` on synthetic v9 lockfiles. pnpm parse plus `--no-dev` filter: n=5,000: 936 + 814 ms; n=10,000: 3,018 + 3,105 ms; n=20,000: 8,477 + 8,463 ms. Yarn Berry at the same sizes: 195 + 192, 363 + 378, and 828 + 760 ms. `yaml.parse` on the n=20,000 pnpm file takes 9,000 ms by default and 1,020 ms with `uniqueKeys: false`. Script: perf-pnpm.mts from the parser review.

## Impact

Large pnpm monorepos wait about 17 s with `--no-dev` at 20k packages, and the cost quadruples each time the lockfile doubles. npm and Yarn lockfiles of the same size take under 2 s.

## Fix

Pass `{ uniqueKeys: false }` in `readLock`, as yarn-berry.ts does; pnpm never writes duplicate keys. Parse once: have `filterDevPackages` take the already-parsed lock, or memoise the last `(content, lock)` pair in `readLock`.

## Resolution
readLock passes uniqueKeys: false to parseAllDocuments and memoises the last (content, lock) pair, so --no-dev reuses the parse. perf-pnpm at n=20,000 went from 8998 + 8675 ms to 1016 + 45 ms (parse + --no-dev). Tests "reads a lockfile that repeats a key" and "parses the same content once" each fail without their part of the fix. Full gate: cov 390/390 at 100%.
title: pnpm lockfile parsing is quadratic in package count and runs twice under --no-dev

body:
## Problem

`extractNameVersion` returns null unless the key has the shape `name@version` (`V6_KEY` or `V9_KEY`). In lockfile v6, non-registry packages are keyed by source instead, for example `github.com/jonschlinkert/is-number/98e8ff…` or `file:../localdep`, and their real name and version are in the entry's `name:` and `version:` fields. `parsePnpmLockfile` skips such keys (pnpm.ts:105-106), so the packages vanish from the analysis. `pnpmInstallSets` (pnpm.ts:165-168) creates no node for them either, so the `--no-dev` walk stops there and drops everything reachable only through them.

## Evidence

Reproduced with pnpm 8.15.9 (`lockfileVersion: '6.0'`). package.json dependencies: `debug@4.3.4`, `localdep: file:../localdep` (engines `node >=22`, depends on `ms@2.1.3`) and `is-number: github:jonschlinkert/is-number#7.0.0`; dev dependency `send@0.18.0`. The lockfile has the keys `file:../localdep` and `github.com/jonschlinkert/is-number/98e8ff…`. The parser lists 21 packages, but neither `localdep@1.0.0` nor `is-number@7.0.0` is among them. `pnpm install --prod` installs 5 packages; `--no-dev` keeps 2 and drops `is-number@7.0.0`, `localdep@1.0.0` and `ms@2.1.3`. The full run and `--no-dev` both report a node intersection of `>=6.0.0` instead of `>=22`. Script: repro-pnpm.sh, section P2.

## Impact

On pnpm 8 lockfiles, the engines of local, git and tarball dependencies are ignored, which can report a Node range far wider than the project supports. `--no-dev` also drops their production dependencies.

## Fix

Pass the entry to the name extractor. When no key pattern matches and the entry has a string `name`, use `{ name: entry.name, version: entry.version ?? stripPeerSuffix(key) }` and mark the package `unpublished`. Use the same helper in `pnpmInstallSets`, so the node exists and the walk continues through it. Add a v6 fixture with a `file:` and a git dependency.

## Resolution
readPackage(key, metaBlock) in pnpm.ts replaces extractNameVersion for both the parser and pnpmInstallSets. An entry with a string `name` (v6 git, tarball or directory) is read from its entry and marked unpublished. This is checked before the key patterns, because real pnpm 8 keys such as file:../../@me/scoped would otherwise misparse; v9 entries carry no name, so v9 output is unchanged. Repro P2: --no-dev now keeps 5 packages instead of 2, and the node intersection is >=22.0.0 instead of >=6.0.0. pnpm 8 writes no version for a directory dependency, so it is labelled localdep@file:../localdep, as the v9 parser already does. Tests fail without the fallback and with key-first order.
title: pnpm lockfile v6 drops git, tarball and directory packages, and --no-dev loses what only they reach

body:
## Problem

In v6 lockfiles the packages block itself is keyed with the peer suffix (`/react-dom@18.2.0(react@18.2.0)`), so metadata is found only through the `?? metaBlock[key]` fallback in `const meta = metaBlock[stripPeerSuffix(key)] ?? metaBlock[key] ?? {}`. Removing that fallback leaves the suite green: the only suffixed v6 key in the tests (`/lodash@4.17.21(peer@1.0.0)`) has no engines or peers to lose, and test/fixtures/pnpm-lock.yaml has no `(`.

## Evidence

pnpm.ts:114. Tests reviewer mutation: removing `?? metaBlock[key]` → 374/374 pass; run directly, `/react-dom@18.2.0(react@18.2.0): {engines: {node: '>=0.10.0'}, peerDependencies: {react: ^18.2.0}}` then parses to `{name, version, hasMetadata: true}` with engines and peers gone.

## Impact

A regression would silently drop engines/peers for every peer-suffixed pnpm v6 package while `hasMetadata: true` suppresses the registry lookup and the offline "no metadata" warning, widening the reported range with no signal.

## Fix

Add to test/parsers/pnpm.test.ts a v6 lockfile with `/a@1.0.0(b@2.0.0):` carrying `engines: {node: '>=18'}` and `peerDependencies: {b: ^2}`, asserting both are kept.

## Resolution
Added test/parsers/pnpm.test.ts "keeps engines and peerDependencies for a peer-suffixed v6 key". It fails when the metadata lookup for suffixed keys is removed.
title: No test checks metadata for pnpm v6 package keys with a peer suffix

body:
## Problem

Edges are looked up by `nodeKey({ name, range })` built from each dependency's declared range (yarn-berry.ts:148-151), and nodes are stored only under their own descriptors (:168). With a root `resolutions` entry, dependents keep listing the original range, while the lockfile holds only the pinned descriptor. The edge lookup misses, so the pinned package and its whole subtree are cut off from the production roots.

## Evidence

Reproduced with Yarn 4.9.2 workspaces: the root has `"resolutions": {"ms": "2.1.3"}`, workspace `a` depends on `debug@4.3.4`, and workspace `b` has dev dependency `send@0.18.0`. In yarn.lock, `debug@npm:4.3.4` lists `ms: "npm:2.1.2"`, but the only ms key is `"ms@npm:2.1.3"`. `yarn workspaces focus --all --production` installs `ms@2.1.3`, and `--no-dev` drops it. Script: repro-yarn.sh, section Y1.

## Impact

Any Yarn Berry project that uses `resolutions`, a common way to force a security fix, under-reports production constraints with `--no-dev`. That can produce an engines range the production install does not satisfy.

## Fix

After building `nodes`, resolve any dependency key with no node to every node of the same package name. This over-approximates, which is consistent with graph/index.ts dropping only packages known to come from a dev install. Alternatively, apply the root manifest's `resolutions` when building edge keys. The same name fallback also fixes the `file:` and `portal:` locator finding from this run.

## Resolution
yarn-berry.ts adds resolver(nodes): a dependency key with no node falls back to every node of the same package name. That over-includes, consistent with graph/index.ts dropping only packages known to come from dev installs. Edges are resolved after all nodes exist. Repro Y1 (Yarn 4.9.2 with resolutions ms 2.1.3): nothing is MISSING any more; before, ms@2.1.3 was dropped. Test "follows a dependency that resolutions pinned to another version" fails without the fallback.
title: Yarn Berry --no-dev drops packages pinned by resolutions

body:
## Problem

Lockfile keys for `file:` and `portal:` dependencies are bound to the workspace that declares them, for example `"localdir@file:./localdir::locator=root%40workspace%3A."`. The workspace entry lists only `localdir: "file:./localdir"`, so the root key `localdir@file:./localdir` built by `nodeKey` (:123-125, pushed at :160-163) never matches a node. The walk stops at that root, and everything the local package depends on is treated as dev-only.

## Evidence

Reproduced with Yarn 4.9.2. Root dependencies: `localdir` (`file:./localdir`, depends on `ms@2.1.2`) and `portaled` (`portal:./portaled`, depends on `debug@2.6.9`). Root dev dependencies: `debug@4.3.4` and `send@0.18.0`. yarn.lock keys are `"localdir@file:./localdir::locator=root%40workspace%3A."` and `"portaled@portal:./portaled::locator=root%40workspace%3A."`. `yarn workspaces focus --all --production` installs `debug@2.6.9`, `ms@2.0.0` and `ms@2.1.2`, and `--no-dev` drops all three. Script: repro-yarn.sh, section Y2.

## Impact

Monorepos and projects with local `file:` or `portal:` packages lose those packages' production dependency constraints under `--no-dev`.

## Fix

When `dep.key` has no node, retry with `` `${dep.key}::locator=${encodeURIComponent(ownerResolution)}` ``, where `ownerResolution` is the declaring entry's resolution: `encodeURIComponent('root@workspace:.')` gives `root%40workspace%3A.`. The name fallback in the resolutions finding from this run also covers this case. Add a test with a `file:` dependency that has its own dependency.

## Resolution
The same name fallback from audit-24f017af resolves workspace-bound ::locator= keys for file: and portal: dependencies. Repro Y2: nothing is MISSING; before, debug@2.6.9, ms@2.0.0 and ms@2.1.2 were dropped. The only line left is the known walker artifact EXTRA portaled@0.0.0-use.local. Test "follows file: and portal: dependencies to what they depend on" uses real ::locator= keys and fails without the fallback.
title: Yarn Berry --no-dev drops production dependencies of file: and portal: dependencies

body:
## Problem

swallowed-exception / masking-fallback. `try { text = readFileSync(file, 'utf8') } catch { continue }` treats every read error like ENOENT, including EACCES (e.g. a root-owned ~/.npmrc left by `sudo npm login`) and EISDIR. The scoped registry settings are lost silently and scoped packages are looked up on the default registry.

## Evidence

client.ts:79-85 (read at the cited range). Reproduced (`scratchpad/review-runtime/npmrc-cases.mjs` case A): project .npmrc with `@corp:registry=<private stub>`, mode 000 → the default-registry stub received `/@corp%2Fsecret-tool/1.0.0` and `/@corp%2Fsecret-tool/latest`, the private stub 0 requests; stderr empty, exit 0. The function's own doc comment says the .npmrc reading exists because private scopes looked up on the default registry "disclosed internal package names to it" (resolved audit-d45e8056).

## Impact

Internal package names are disclosed to the public registry with no signal, exactly the leak the .npmrc support was added to stop.

## Fix

`catch (err: unknown) { if ((err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === 'ENOENT') continue; throw new Error(\`cannot read ${file}: ${(err as Error).message}\`, { cause: err }) }` — fail before any request. This changes the CLI's error contract (a new exit-1 path), so include it in the breaking-change note of audit-cd19913e. Add a test with an unreadable (mode 000) project .npmrc.

## Resolution
readRegistries (client.ts) skips only ENOENT. Any other read error throws `cannot read <file>: <message>` with cause, before any request, online or offline. Test "fails before any request on a .npmrc it cannot read" uses mode 000, checks zero fetch calls, and is skipped as root or on Windows. README "Private registries and proxies" documents the exit 1. This is a new exit-1 path for the breaking-change note in audit-cd19913e.
title: An unreadable .npmrc is treated as absent, so private scoped names go to the default registry

body:
## Problem

key-collision. Online, `processBatch` returns `unpublished` packages untouched (they are never looked up). `resolveOffline` has no such guard: it reads `getVersionData(\`${prefix}${pkg.name}@${pkg.version}\`)` and `getLatestData` for every package and overrides the lockfile's own engines/peers with whatever an unrelated public package of the same name and version left in the cache. The cache key has no "came from a registry" dimension.

## Evidence

client.ts:281-301 (no `unpublished` check) vs :249-255 (online early return). Reproduced (`scratchpad/review-runtime/offline-unpublished.mjs`): workspace member `utils@1.0.0` declaring `engines.node: ">=20"`, cache holding entries from the public `utils`: `--offline` reports range `>=0.8` plus a latest `9.9.9 >=4`; online reports `>=20` and no latest entry.

## Impact

The offline safe range silently widens (or narrows) based on a different package, and an invented "latest" appears for a package that has no registry release.

## Fix

At the top of the `resolveOffline` map add `if (pkg.unpublished === true) { if (pkg.hasMetadata !== true) failures.push(\`${pkg.name}@${pkg.version} (not from a registry)\`); return pkg }`, mirroring processBatch. Add an offline test with an unpublished package and a colliding cache entry.

## Resolution
New isUnpublished() guard in client.ts is shared by processBatch and resolveOffline. Offline, unpublished packages never take registry cache entries, and those with no metadata are reported as "(not from a registry)", matching online. Test "leaves unpublished packages alone offline despite colliding cache entries" (workspace member and git package) fails without the guard.
title: --offline applies registry cache entries to workspace, git and local packages

body:
## Problem

fail-open-default. `resolveOffline` reports a package only when the version manifest is missing (`if (manifest === null && pkg.hasMetadata !== true)`); a missing `getLatestData` entry is never counted. Online, a failed latest lookup is named in the warning. Offline, the latest range is computed from whichever packages happen to have a cached latest entry, and with none the table states "no constraints found" when the truth is "unknown".

## Evidence

client.ts:286-289 (read at the cited range). ## Problem

AUD:S8. `const everyRequestTimedOut = context.timedOut - timedOutBefore === batch.length * 2` assumes every package sends two requests. Cache hits and `unpublished` packages send none, so a batch where every request that was actually sent timed out does not count as stalled. Version entries never expire and latest entries expire after 24 h, so any run a day after a full run sends only the `/latest` requests and the breaker cannot fire; the same holds for any batch containing a workspace or git package.

## Evidence

client.ts:327-341 (read at the cited range). Reproduced by the runtime reviewer with 16 packages against a server that accepts connections and never answers (`scratchpad/review-runtime/stall.mjs`): cold cache stops after 20.1 s with the "stopped responding" warning; warm version cache runs 40.1 s, every batch waits the full 10 s, no warning — extrapolated about 83 minutes for 2,000 packages. This is a gap in the fix for resolved audit-836fda13.

## Impact

On a filtered or blackholed network with a warm cache, the CLI hangs for an hour-plus on a large lockfile instead of stopping after two batches, which is what the breaker exists to prevent.

## Fix

Count requests actually sent: add `requests: number` to LookupContext and `context.requests++` in `fetchDocument` before `fetch`; per batch compute `const sent = context.requests - requestsBefore; const timedOut = context.timedOut - timedOutBefore; stalledBatches = sent > 0 && timedOut === sent ? stalledBatches + 1 : (sent > 0 ? 0 : stalledBatches)`. Add a test with a pre-filled version cache and a never-answering stub asserting the run stops after MAX_STALLED_BATCHES.

## Resolution
LookupContext.requests counts requests actually sent. A batch counts as stalled when sent > 0 and every sent request timed out; a batch that sends nothing neither counts nor resets the streak. Test "stops at a stalled registry when the version lookups are cached" fails without the fix: all 40 calls go out and nothing is skipped.

## Problem

Over-reporting coverage. The `?? pkg.version` side of `version: pkg.latestVersion ?? pkg.version` (line 312) never runs in any test, yet `npm run cov` reports 100% branches. Node's built-in merge (`mergeCoverageRanges` in lib/internal/test_runner/coverage.js) drops the nested zero-count range once it finds an exact match for the enclosing block in a coverage dump from a spawned CLI child process, so the branch is counted as covered. The branch is also unreachable in production: `latestEngines`/`latestPeerDependencies` are only set together with `latestVersion` from the same validated `latest` object (src/registry/client.ts:260-267, :290-301).

## Evidence

Reproduced: running every test file except test/cli.test.ts with `--test-reporter=lcov` gives `BRDA:312,91,0,0` (branch never taken) for intersect.ts; the full `test/**/*.test.ts` run emits no BRDA entry for line 312 at all, and `npm run cov` reports 100.00 branches. Tests reviewer: instrumenting the fallback to log never fired across 374 tests, and a mutant that throws on that side survived 374/374; replaying Node's merge (`scratchpad/review-quality/nodemerge.mjs`) shows the zero range vanishing at the 8th merged dump. Using a correct per-byte merge of the raw V8 dumps, this is the only never-executed span in src.

## Impact

The coverage gate the project relies on ("fails below 100%") can report full coverage for code no test runs, the over-reporting the owner explicitly asked to rule out; any future branch reached only by unit tests but enclosed by a block the CLI children execute can hide the same way.

## Fix

Remove the unreachable fallback by making the type say what the client guarantees: replace `latestVersion`, `latestEngines`, `latestPeerDependencies` on Package with `latest?: { version: string; engines?: Record<string,string>; peerDependencies?: Record<string,string> }` and read `pkg.latest.version` here. Guard against the merge flaw itself by adding a CI check that runs coverage once without test/cli.test.ts and fails on any `BRDA:...,0` line that the full run omits (or switch the gate to c8, whose merge keeps nested zero-count ranges). Document the limitation in CONTRIBUTING.md's coverage paragraph.

## Resolution
Package.latest?: { version, engines?, peerDependencies? } replaces the three latest* fields across src and tests. intersect.ts reads pkg.latest.version, and the unreachable `?? pkg.version` fallback is deleted. New .github/scripts/coverage-merge-guard.mjs, run in ci.yml after npm run cov, fails when a never-taken BRDA from the run without test/cli.test.ts has no entry in the full run. On a scratch rebuild of the pre-refactor code it flagged src/analyzer/intersect.ts:312; on the current tree it passes. The guard also exposed table.ts:4's columns fallback, now pinned by unit tests (columns = 0). CONTRIBUTING.md documents the guard. cov 390/390 at 100%.
title: The 100% branch gate passes with a branch no test executes, hidden by Node's subprocess coverage merge

## Problem

The version is taken from the key (`const { name, version } = parsed`, pnpm.ts:107). For a v9 git or tarball package, the key's version part is the source URL, while the entry's `version:` field holds the real version. That URL is shown as the version, and `resolveLocal` (src/registry/local.ts:43) skips the installed manifest because its version can never equal the URL.

## Evidence

Reproduced with pnpm 12.6.0 and the dependency `is-number: github:jonschlinkert/is-number#7.0.0`. The lockfile entry is `is-number@https://codeload.github.com/jonschlinkert/is-number/tar.gz/98e8ff…:` with `version: 7.0.0`. The parser emits `is-number@https://codeload.github.com/jonschlinkert/is-number/tar.gz/98e8ff…` (unpublished). npm, Yarn Classic and Yarn Berry all report `is-number@7.0.0` for the same dependency. Script: repro-pnpm.sh, section P3.

## Impact

The output shows a long URL instead of the version for pnpm git and tarball dependencies. The local node_modules pass also cannot enrich them, so their engines and peers come from the lockfile entry only.

## Fix

Use `meta.version` when it is a string and fall back to the key's version. Keep `unpublished: true` decided from the key's reference, not the display version; otherwise `7.0.0` would look like a registry version and be fetched from the public registry. Build the `--no-dev` ids in `pnpmInstallSets` with the same helper, so the ids stay equal.

## Resolution
readPackage's key-pattern branch uses meta.version ?? keyVersion, and unpublished is still decided from the key's version. Repro P3: is-number@7.0.0, unpublished; before, it showed the codeload URL. Parser and graph tests fail without the fix, and the parser test fails if unpublished is derived from the display version.
title: pnpm v9 reports the source URL as the version of git and tarball packages

## Problem

Masking fallback (AUD:S6). `projectManifests` reads each workspace member with `readProjectManifest(...).deps ?? []`, so a member whose package.json is malformed or unreadable is dropped without a word. Its production dependencies stop being roots; any package they reach that another member lists as a devDependency is then classed dev-only and removed by `--no-dev`. The root manifest gets the opposite treatment (src/cli.ts:214-218 throws "--no-dev needs a readable package.json"), precisely because an unfiltered or wrongly filtered result would be labelled production-only.

## Evidence

Reproduced with Node 26.10.0 (scratch project: root `workspaces: ["packages/*"]`; packages/a/package.json = `{"name":"a","version":"1.0.0","dependencies":{"lodash":"^4.17.0"}` (missing closing brace); packages/b/package.json has `devDependencies: {lodash: ^4.17.0}`; yarn.lock has `lodash@^4.17.0` → 4.17.21):
- `filterDevPackages(...)` returns `[]`; with a's manifest fixed it returns `["lodash"]`.
- `semver-ranger --no-dev --offline` prints `semver-ranger — analyzing 0 packages` and no warning.
Yarn Berry's equivalent (src/parsers/yarn-berry.ts:154-163) falls back to counting every dependency as production, the safe direction.

## Impact

A production dependency's engines/peer constraints vanish from the `--no-dev` report with nothing telling the user, so the reported safe range is wider than what the production install needs. Requires a malformed or unreadable member package.json, which is uncommon but is exactly the state an in-progress edit leaves.

## Fix

Treat an unusable member manifest the way the root is treated: in `projectManifests`, when `readProjectManifest(memberDir).error !== null`, throw `new Error(\`--no-dev needs a readable package.json in ${memberDir}: ${error}\`)` (ENOENT already yields `error: null` and stays skipped). Add a graph test with a malformed member manifest asserting the throw, next to the existing "unreadable"/"empty" workspace cases in test/graph/index.test.ts.

## Resolution
projectManifests (yarn-classic.ts) throws "--no-dev needs a readable package.json in <memberDir>: <error>" for a malformed, unreadable or null member manifest; ENOENT is still skipped. The graph tests replace the old test that asserted the bug, and fail without the fix. filterDevPackages and README document it. This is a new exit-1 path for the breaking-change note.
title: Yarn Classic --no-dev silently drops a workspace whose package.json is unusable

## Problem

Finding class: sast (terminal escape injection). The table strips control characters from lockfile and registry text (src/output/table.ts wrap, the fix for audit-a1f69e2e), but two stderr paths print the same untrusted text raw: `warnUnresolved` joins failure labels built from lockfile package names (`console.error(\`  ${named}...\`)`, src/cli.ts:168), and the top-level handler prints parser error messages (`console.error('Error:', (err as Error).message)`, src/cli.ts:301), which for YAML lockfiles quote the offending source line.

## Evidence

Detected by manual review during the security deep-run; no scanner rule covers it. Reproduced with Node 26.10.0:
1. yarn.lock with header `"evil\u001b]52;c;aGFja2Vk\u0007\u001b[2J@^1.0.0":` (version 1.0.0), `npm_config_registry=http://127.0.0.1:9`, run `semver-ranger`: stderr line 2 is `  evil^[]52;c;aGFja2Vk^G^[[2J@1.0.0 (network error), ...` (cat -v), i.e. a raw OSC 52 clipboard write and a clear-screen sequence. stdout contains no ESC byte.
2. pnpm-lock.yaml with line `  a: b: \u001b]0;pwned\u0007\u001b[2J`, run `semver-ranger --offline`: exit 1, stderr `Error: Nested mappings are not allowed ... a: b: ^[]0;pwned^G^[[2J`.
JSON lockfile/package.json parse errors do not echo input and are unaffected; `--json` output is safe because JSON.stringify escapes control characters.

## Impact

Running the CLI on an untrusted checkout (its intended use, including in CI logs viewed in a terminal) lets the lockfile author drive the terminal: clear or rewrite earlier output, set the window title, or, on terminals that honour OSC 52 writes, replace the clipboard. The table-side fix documents exactly this threat, so the stderr gap leaves the stated defence incomplete.

## Fix

Strip C0/C1 control characters except newline from every stderr message that can carry external text: add one helper in src/cli.ts, e.g. `const printable = (text: string): string => text.replace(/[^\P{Cc}\n]/gu, '')`, and apply it in `warnUnresolved` (summary and `named`), in the `main().catch` handler and the parseArgs error handler, and to `manifest.error`/flush failure messages. Add CLI tests that feed an ESC-bearing yarn.lock name and an ESC-bearing malformed pnpm-lock.yaml and assert stderr contains no `\u001b`.

## Resolution
New report() in cli.ts strips control characters except newline, and every stderr write in cli.ts goes through it. CLI tests feed an ESC-bearing yarn.lock name and an ESC-bearing malformed pnpm-lock.yaml; both fail without the fix.
title: Lockfile text reaches stderr with terminal escape sequences intact

## Problem

context-free-error (AUD:S21). When reading or parsing the lockfile fails, the catch block calls `parseSpinner.fail(\`Parsing ${lockfileBase}\`)` and rethrows the raw error; the top-level handler prints only `Error: <message>`. The spinner is a no-op when stderr is not a TTY (src/output/progress.ts), so in CI and any piped run the message is the parser's own text, which for JSON lockfiles names no file at all.

## Evidence

Reproduced with Node 26.10.0, stderr not a TTY:
- package-lock.json = `{"lockfileVersion": 3, "packages": {` → stderr `Error: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 36 (line 1 column 37)`, exit 1.
- pnpm-lock.yaml with `snapshots: [` → `Error: Flow sequence in block collection must be sufficiently indented ... at line 3, column 1:` (no file name).
Only the EACCES case names the path, because Node's fs error message contains it.

## Impact

A failing CI job reports a JSON/YAML position with no file, in a directory that can hold package.json, several lockfiles, or a positional path the user passed; the user has to guess which file is broken. Non-critical path, so Low.

## Fix

In the catch block wrap the error with the path before rethrowing: `throw new Error(\`could not read ${lockfilePath}: ${(err as Error).message}\`, { cause: err })`. Add a CLI test that runs against a truncated package-lock.json with stderr piped and asserts the message contains `package-lock.json`.

## Resolution
The parse catch rethrows "could not read <path>: <message>" with cause. The CLI test with piped stderr asserts the file name and no stack, and fails without the fix.
title: A lockfile parse error names no file outside a terminal

## Problem

cause-destroyed. `console.error('Error:', (err as Error).message)` prints only the message for every error, including TypeErrors from malformed input reaching code that does not guard it, so a bug report has no file, line or entry.

## Evidence

cli.ts:301. Reproduced (`scratchpad/review-runtime/toplevel-error.mjs`): a package-lock.json entry `"node_modules/a": null` prints only `Error: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'version')`.

Crashes on unusual lockfiles cannot be traced from the report a user files.

`if (err instanceof Error && err.name !== 'Error') console.error(err.stack); else console.error('Error:', (err as Error).message)` — the CLI's own errors are plain `Error` and keep the one-line message. Add a CLI test with the null entry asserting a stack line. (The null entry itself is a parser robustness bug; see the parser findings.)

## Resolution
isBug() in cli.ts prints the inspected error with its stack for TypeError, RangeError or ReferenceError, thrown directly or as the cause of the parse wrapper. Plain Error and malformed-input SyntaxError or YAMLParseError keep the one-line message: the finding's `name !== 'Error'` rule would have dumped stacks for bad lockfiles. Fault-injection CLI tests fail without the fix.

## Problem

`detectLockfile` looks only for `package-lock.json` (detect.ts:52), and `resolveLockfile` in src/cli.ts:93-95 accepts that basename only. npm-shrinkwrap.json has the same format and takes precedence over package-lock.json in npm, but it is not recognised.

Projects that publish with a shrinkwrap cannot be analysed. When both files exist, the tool analyses package-lock.json, which npm ignores in that case.

In `detectLockfile`, check `npm-shrinkwrap.json` before `package-lock.json`. Accept that basename in `resolveLockfile` with type `npm`; `parseNpmLockfile` already handles the format. Update the README's list of supported lockfiles.

npm-shrinkwrap.json comes first in LOCKFILE_NAMES and maps to npm, so it wins over package-lock.json in auto-detection and is accepted as an explicit path. CLI matrix and detect tests (including precedence) fail without the fix. README lists the format and the precedence.

## Problem

Peer edges come from the packages' `peerDependencies` (yarn-classic.ts:186), which yarn.lock does not store. src/cli.ts:214-219 runs `filterDevPackages` after the `node_modules` pass but before the registry pass. Without `node_modules`, no peer data exists yet when the filter runs, even online. The README documents the limitation, but the run order causes it and could be changed.

## Evidence

Reproduced with Yarn 1.22.22: dependencies `react-dom@18.2.0`, dev dependencies `react@18.2.0`. `yarn install --production` installs `react@18.2.0`. With node_modules present, `--no-dev` keeps react. After `rm -rf node_modules`, `--no-dev` drops `react@18.2.0`. Script: repro-yarn.sh, section Y3.

## Impact

In a fresh CI checkout or before install, `--no-dev` on Yarn Classic omits peer-installed packages such as react, so their engines and peer ranges are missing from the production result.

## Fix

For yarn-classic, run `filterDevPackages` after `resolveRegistry`. The registry pass then resolves dev packages that are later dropped, which costs requests only, not correctness. Alternatively, filter, resolve, add back any dev root that a kept package names as a peer, then resolve those and filter again. Then remove the README caveat.

## Resolution
For yarn-classic, cli.ts runs filterDevPackages after the registry pass, so peer data from the registry or cache reaches the filter; yarn-classic.ts is unchanged. CLI test (stand-in registry; react-dom peers react; no node_modules) fails without the fix. README's caveat now says only an offline run with no node_modules or cache misses such a package. Trade-off: dev packages are looked up before being dropped.

## Problem

AUD:B0. The latest version is looked up in `target.latestRanges`, which only contains packages whose latest version still declares the constraint. When the latest release removes it, the row shows `—`, hiding the upgrade that lifts the restriction.

## Evidence

table.ts:197 `new Map(target.latestRanges.map(r => [r.package, r]))`, :200 `renderPackageRow(ui, entry, latest?.version ?? '—')`. Reproduced (`scratchpad/review-runtime/table-cases.mjs`): `foo@1.0.0 >=12` with latest `3.0.0` declaring no engines renders `foo  1.0.0  —  >=12`.

## Impact

The most useful upgrade hint (the latest release has no restriction) is shown as "unknown".

## Fix

Measured by the runtime reviewer (`scratchpad/review-runtime/perf-intersect.mjs`) with one outlier forcing the full search: `analyzeEngines` 228 ms for 526 packages, 904 ms for 2,101, 2,335 ms for 5,251; synthetic 5,000 entries with 200 distinct ranges: 3.7 s.

## Impact

Seconds of CPU on large monorepo lockfiles, most visible with a warm cache when the network costs nothing. No wrong results.

## Fix

Group entries by normalized range and fold each group once; identical ranges always get the same accept/reject decision within a run, so results are unchanged and cost drops to distinct-ranges². Keep the existing brute-force intersect tests as the guard.

## Resolution
greedyFrom (intersect.ts) decides each normalized range once per seed run and applies that verdict to every entry sharing it, keeping input order. Once accepted, later combined ranges lie inside the range; once rejected, inside the range it failed against. So results are identical. Synthetic bench with one outlier forcing the full search: 5,000 entries / 200 ranges went from 3758 ms to 508 ms, and 2,000 / 100 from 777 ms to 209 ms, with the same output. All existing intersect tests pass, plus a guard test for differently spelled equal ranges.
title: Conflict search re-folds every entry for every distinct seed range

## Problem

Unenforced rule. .claude/rules/ci-ignore-scripts.md: "Install with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in every workflow." No hook, linter, CI step or npm setting backs it. The rule is the only barrier between dependency lifecycle scripts and the publish job, which holds `id-token: write` (npm trusted publishing) and `contents: write`. The rule file is also untracked (see the agent-rules finding on .claude/), so it does not load anywhere except this machine.

## Evidence

Constructed bypass on a scratch copy of .github/workflows: `perl -pi -e 's/npm ci --ignore-scripts/npm ci/' publish.yml`, which turns line 60 into `- run: npm ci`. Then actionlint 1.7.12 gives 0 findings, `zizmor --pedantic` gives 0, and `checkov --framework github_actions` gives 0 failed. CI runs no check for the flag, and .npmrc does not set `ignore-scripts`. The same edit on ci.yml:40/90 or pr-lint.yml:53 is equally invisible.

## Impact

One reviewed-in edit, or an agent session without the local rule, lets any dependency's install script run in the job that can mint an npm OIDC token and push tags, so a compromised transitive dev dependency could publish a tampered @ivuorinen/semver-ranger with provenance.

## Fix

Make it the default rather than a flag to remember: add `ignore-scripts=true` to the project .npmrc. Every `npm ci`/`npm install` in every workflow, and locally, then skips dependency lifecycle scripts even when the flag is missing. `npm run`/`npm test` still run their named script (only pre/post hooks are skipped, and package.json defines none), and `npm publish` has no lifecycle scripts here. Keep the explicit flags as documentation. Prove closure by re-running the scratch bypass and showing `npm ci` (no flag) in a throwaway project with a postinstall dependency does not run it.

## Resolution
.npmrc sets ignore-scripts=true, so every npm ci/install in every workflow and locally skips dependency lifecycle scripts even when the flag is dropped. Closure proven in a throwaway project: a file: dependency's postinstall ran under plain `npm ci` without the setting and did not run with it; `npm test` still ran its named script. `npm config get ignore-scripts` from the repo root resolves true.
title: Nothing enforces --ignore-scripts in workflows, so dropping it from the publish job (id-token: write) passes every check

## Problem

serialization-drift. `setVersionData` keeps `engines` and `peerDependencies` only when `isRanges` holds, meaning every value is a string, and `getVersionData` rejects an entry otherwise. One non-string value, such as `npm: 7`, therefore discards its valid siblings like `node: '>=14'` from the cached entry. `fetchManifest` returns the unfiltered manifest to the current run (src/registry/client.ts:244-249), so the cold run analyses the real constraints and every later run, online or offline, analyses the filtered copy. The docstring's premise, "the analysis reads only an object of ranges anyway", is false: `rangeText` in src/analyzer/intersect.ts:274-276 deliberately renders non-string values as "not a string: …" so they stay visible. `getLatestData` has the opposite gap, validating no field shapes at all.

## Evidence

cache/index.ts:121: `(isRecord(value) && Object.values(value).every(range => typeof range === 'string'))`. Lines 155-158 store a field only `...(isRanges(data.engines) && { engines: data.engines })`. Reproduced: `setVersionData('a@1', { engines: { node: '>=14', npm: 7 } })` then `getVersionData('a@1')` returns `{}`. End to end, against a local registry serving `a@1.0.0` with `engines: {node: '>=14', npm: 7}` and `b@1.0.0` with `engines: {node: '>=12'}`, the cold run reports node ranges `a >=14, b >=12`, intersection `>=14.0.0`, and the npm target's invalid range `not a string: 7`. The warm run with the same cache dir reports only `b >=12`, intersection `>=12.0.0`, no npm target, and no warning.

## Impact

The second and every later run silently report a more permissive safe range than the first, the failure the tool exists to prevent and that .claude/rules/no-silent-degradation.md forbids. The cache keeps the bad entry indefinitely, because version entries never expire.

## Fix

Validate shape, not value types: replace `isRanges` with `const isConstraintMap = (v: unknown) => typeof v === 'undefined' || isRecord(v)`. Use it in `setVersionData` (still dropping the string and array `engines` of old releases, which the analyzer ignores anyway), in `getVersionData`, and in `getLatestData` alongside `isFresh`, so both stores accept and reject the same shapes. Have `fetchManifest` return the stored object so cold and warm runs see identical data. Add a child-process test in test/cache/ asserting that the entry `{ engines: { node: '>=14', npm: 7 } }` round-trips unchanged and that a CLI run against it gives the same JSON cold and warm. This deliberately changes one existing expectation: test/cache/limits.test.ts:64-84 asserts that `'numeric-range@1.0.0': { peerDependencies: { react: 18 } }` reads back as `null`, which encodes this drift. It should read back as the stored entry, so the analysis can show `not a string: 18`. The `'string-engines@1.0.0'` and `'garbage@1.0.0'` cases stay `null`.

## Resolution
cache/index.ts validates shape only (isConstraintMap: absent or an object) in getVersionData and isFresh; constraintFields keeps object fields for both stores; setVersionData/setLatestData return what they store and fetchManifest/fetchLatest return that, so cold and warm runs see the same data. limits.test.ts numeric-range expectation changed from null to the entry (it encoded the drift); new tests: mixed-engines round-trip, latest string-engines rejected, latest fields stored and returned, CLI cold vs warm same node target (>=14.0.0). Proven: reverting to the value check fails the round-trip test.
title: The version cache drops a whole engines or peers object when any value is not a string, so a warm run reports a wider range than the cold run

body:
## Problem

AUD:S4. `resolveRegistry` slices the packages into batches of 4 and awaits each batch's `Promise.all` before starting the next. Up to 8 requests are in flight, but a batch lasts as long as its slowest request, so one tail-latency response idles the other 7 slots. Throughput is set by the tail latency, not the mean. The concurrency cap ("stay within ~8 total concurrent network requests") does not need this: a sliding pool keeps the same cap without the idle slots.

## Evidence

client.ts:416-420: `for (let i = 0; i < packages.length; i += CONCURRENCY) { const batch = packages.slice(i, i + CONCURRENCY) ... const resolved = await processBatch(batch, context)`. Measured against a local registry (npm_config_registry) with deterministic per-URL latency, 90% of requests at 50 ms and 10% at 600 ms, for 200 uncached packages (400 requests): the CLI took 15,598 ms. The lockstep model predicts 15,150 ms and an 8-wide sliding pool over the same latencies 5,000 ms.

## Impact

Every cold-cache run pays about 3x the necessary wall time on a registry with ordinary tail latency. That includes every CI run, because the cache directory is not persisted between jobs. On a 2,000-package lockfile it is minutes of avoidable waiting behind the spinner.

## Fix

Replace the batch loop with a pool of CONCURRENCY workers, each pulling the next package index from a shared counter and calling the existing per-package body of `processBatch`, so a slot refills as soon as its package completes. Keep results in input order by writing to `result[index]`. Move the stall breaker from batches to requests: count consecutive timed-out requests, reset on any request that did not time out, stop handing out work once the count reaches `MAX_STALLED_BATCHES * CONCURRENCY * 2`, and mark the remainder skipped as now. Keep the existing stalled-registry tests passing, and add one asserting that a single slow package does not delay its batch neighbours, e.g. by checking request start times against a mock fetch.

## Resolution
resolveRegistry runs CONCURRENCY workers pulling from a shared iterator; per-package tallies drive a breaker that stops handing out work after MAX_STALLED_PACKAGES (8) consecutive packages whose every request timed out (packages sending nothing neither count nor reset); a thrown lookup stops other workers. Measured with the same local-registry simulation: 15,598 ms before, 7,651 ms after (remaining gap to 5,000 ms is per-package granularity, marked ponytail). Stall/progress tests updated to exact pool values (22/11 calls, packages 11+ skipped, per-package progress); new tests: next package starts while a slow one is in flight, workers stop after a throw. Proven: a lockstep-batch revert fails the in-flight test.
title: Registry lookups run in lockstep batches, so each batch waits for its slowest request; cold runs take about 3x longer than the same concurrency allows

Lines 29-31: `const args = words[0] === 'git' ? words.slice(1) : words` / `if (!['rm', 'mv'].includes(tool)) return null`.

## Impact

Low blast radius: a deletion through any of these forms leaves references behind unprompted, the recurrence the hook was added to stop.

## Fix

Normalise the command word with `basename(words[0])`, skip git's global options (`-C <dir>`, `-c <k=v>`) before reading the subcommand, add `unlink` (all operands removed), treat `xargs` by recursing into its trailing words, and for `find` with `-delete` ask unconditionally, since its targets are not resolvable statically. Prove closure by re-feeding the five inputs above and showing `ask`.

## Resolution
deleted-path-refs.mjs matches commands by basename, skips git global options (-C, -c, --git-dir, --work-tree, --namespace), handles unlink, and asks unconditionally for xargs rm/mv/unlink and find -delete / -exec rm, whose targets are known only at run time. Closure re-fed: unlink, git -C . rm, find -delete, xargs rm, /bin/rm, find -exec rm, git -c ... mv all return ask; rm -rf dist (untracked), find without delete, xargs wc, git status allowed.
title: deleted-path-refs only recognises rm/mv as the first word, so unlink, git -C, find -delete and xargs rm delete referenced files silently

## Problem

AUD:B0. The satisfiability check added for audit-b8857100 calls `semver.minVersion` on the whole combined range. semver's minVersion takes the lowest candidate across all OR-sets and tests only that one, so it returns null whenever the lowest set is itself unsatisfiable, even when a later set matches. The seed enters `greedyFrom` unchecked (`let combined = seed.range`, line 150), so a seed carrying a dead OR-branch reaches this check intact when nothing else is folded into it.

## Evidence

src/analyzer/intersect.ts:254: `if (semver.minVersion(best.combined) === null) { return { intersection: null, conflicts: [...best.accepted, ...best.conflicts], invalid } }`. Reproduced: `computeIntersection([{package:'p',version:'1',range:'>=20.0.0 <18.0.0 || >=22.0.0'}])` returns `{"intersection":null,"conflicts":[{"package":"p",...}]}`, although `>=22.0.0` satisfies the range. Adding a second entry `>=21` makes `andRanges` drop the dead group and the result becomes `>=22.0.0`, so the answer depends on whether another package happens to declare a constraint.

## Impact

The table shows "conflict — no safe range" and lists the package as conflicting with itself, for a constraint that can be met. That holds for the installed or latest side whenever a single package declares that target.

## Fix

Normalise the seed the way every other entry is normalised, so dead groups are dropped before the check: in greedyFrom, `let combined = andRanges(seed.range, '*') ?? seed.range`. A fully unsatisfiable seed keeps its text, and line 254 still reports it, so audit-b8857100 stays fixed. Add the reproduction above to test/analyzer/intersect.test.ts, expecting `>=22.0.0`.

## Resolution
intersect.ts greedyFrom seeds from liveGroups(seed.range), which drops unsatisfiable OR-groups group by group (keeping each group's comparators, so prerelease permissions survive; ANDing with '*' broke two prerelease tests and was not used). Test: `>=20.0.0 <18.0.0 || >=22.0.0` alone gives intersection >=22.0.0, no conflicts; the lone-unsatisfiable test still passes. Proven: reverting fails the new test.
title: A lone satisfiable range with one unsatisfiable OR-branch is reported as a conflict

## Problem

AUD:S0. .claude/rules/terminal-safe-output.md: "Strip control characters from lockfile and registry text before writing it to stdout or stderr." `report()` strips every Cc character except `\n`, which it keeps because the bug path prints a multi-line `inspect(error)`. Package names, versions and parser excerpts from the lockfile reach `report` through `warnUnresolved`, the error message and the skipped and latest warnings, so a `\n` inside one starts a new stderr line whose content the lockfile chooses. The table path is safe: `wrap()` strips all of `\p{Cc}`, `\n` included.

## Evidence

src/cli.ts:37: `console.error(message.replace(/[^\P{Cc}\n]/gu, ''))`. Reproduced: a v1 package-lock.json with the dependency key `"evil\nWarning: all 312 lookups resolved; ranges are exact."`, run with `--offline`, prints on stderr a standalone line `Warning: all 312 lookups resolved; ranges are exact.@1.0.0 (no metadata)` between the real warnings.

## Impact

A lockfile in a repository someone is asked to review can print counterfeit reassurance, or counterfeit errors, among the tool's real warnings, which is the class of output manipulation the rule exists to stop. No escape sequence is needed, and the only precondition is a crafted lockfile.

## Fix

Sanitise the untrusted text itself, not the finished output. Make `report` replace every control character, `\n` included, with a space: `console.error(message.replace(/\p{Cc}/gu, ' '))`. That closes the reproduced path (`warnUnresolved`) and every other single-line warning. The bug path is the one legitimately multi-line output: write it as `console.error(inspect(error).split('\n').map(line => line.replace(/\p{Cc}/gu, ' ')).join('\n'))`. A newline inside a crash message still breaks a line there, because `error.stack` captured the message at construction, but that output is already visibly a stack trace. Add a CLI test with the reproduction above, asserting that no stderr line starts with the injected text. The existing escape tests cannot catch this: test/cli.test.ts:316 defines `NOT_PRINTABLE = /[^\P{Cc}\n]/u`, which exempts `\n` exactly as `report` does.

## Resolution
Fixed at the source rather than in report(): cli.ts oneLine() turns newlines into spaces in lockfile/package.json text that single-line warnings embed (failure labels in warnUnresolved, manifest errors); report() still strips other control characters and keeps newlines for parser frames and stack traces, which the finding's report()-wide fix would have mangled. CLI test: a lockfile key with an embedded newline prints `evil Warning: ...@1.0.0 (no metadata)` on one line and no stderr line starts with the forged text. Proven: reverting oneLine fails it.
title: report() keeps newlines, so lockfile-controlled names can forge lines on stderr

## Problem

AUD:S17. README.md tells contributors to `npm install`. CONTRIBUTING.md:18-24 says `nvm use` then `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, explaining that `--ignore-scripts` "matches CI and skips the starter-config scripts of the @ivuorinen/* config packages". A contributor who follows the README gets an install that differs from CI's: possible lockfile churn in their first PR, dependency lifecycle scripts run on their machine, and `npm run cov` failing on a non-.nvmrc Node.

Replace the README block with the CONTRIBUTING one (`nvm use` then `npm ci --ignore-scripts`), or keep only `git clone` plus a pointer: "then follow Setup in CONTRIBUTING.md", so there is one source of truth.

README Development now says `nvm use` then `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, as CI does, and points to CONTRIBUTING.md; prettier and markdownlint clean.

## Problem

AUD:S13 (supply-chain execution surface). The hooks CONTRIBUTING.md:41-43 asks contributors to install with `prek install` run code fetched from `https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks` at `rev: v6.0.0`. A tag can be moved to a different commit, so the code that runs on each contributor's `git commit` is whatever the tag points at when prek first clones it. Every third-party action in .github/workflows is pinned to a full commit SHA with the version in a comment (e.g. ci.yml:27 `actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1`). The hook config is the one third-party code path outside that policy.

## Evidence

.pre-commit-config.yaml:4-5: `- repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks` / `rev: v6.0.0`. CI does not run these hooks (CONTRIBUTING.md:42), so nothing reviews what the tag resolves to.

## Impact

A retagged release of the hook repository runs on contributors' machines with their git credentials and working tree, outside the review that the SHA pins give the workflows.

## Fix

Pin by commit: `prek autoupdate --freeze` (or `pre-commit autoupdate --freeze`) rewrites the entry to `rev: <40-char sha>  # frozen: v6.0.0`. Keep Renovate's pre-commit manager able to update it, which understands frozen revs.

.pre-commit-config.yaml pins pre-commit-hooks to 3e8a8703264a2f4a69428a0aa4dcb512790b2c8c (`git ls-remote` of the lightweight v6.0.0 tag) with `# frozen: v6.0.0`; `prek validate-config` and v8r against the schemastore schema both pass.
title: The pre-commit hook repository is pinned by a movable tag, unlike every GitHub Action in this repo

## Problem

AUD:B0. `REGISTRY_RANGE = /^(?:npm|patch):/u` assumes "A patch is applied to a registry package". Yarn's patch protocol wraps any source: the inner range after `patch:<name>@` is the URL-encoded original (`npm%3A5.0.4` for a registry package, `https%3A//github.com/...` for git, `file%3A...` for a local path). A patched non-registry package therefore loses `unpublished`, which src/types.ts:7-11 exists to set because a registry lookup "could only fail or find an unrelated package, and would disclose the name".

## Evidence

yarn-berry.ts:115: `...(!REGISTRY_RANGE.test(range) && { unpublished: true })`. Reproduced: a lockfile entry with resolution `"foo@patch:foo@https%3A//github.com/me/foo.git%23commit=abc#./.yarn/patches/foo.patch::version=1.0.0&hash=1&locator=root%40workspace%3A."` parses to `{"name":"foo","version":"1.0.0"}`, with no `unpublished`. The unpatched git entry `bar@https://github.com/me/bar.git` in the same file parses with `"unpublished":true`.

## Impact

Online, the patched package's name and version go to the configured registry. If a public package shares the name, its engines and peers are analysed in place of the real package's, so the reported range can be wrong in either direction.

## Fix

Decide a patch by its inner source: `const isRegistry = (range: string) => range.startsWith('npm:') || (range.startsWith('patch:') && decodeURIComponent(range.slice(range.indexOf('@', 'patch:'.length + 1) + 1)).startsWith('npm:'))`, which skips a scoped name's leading `@`. Use it in place of `REGISTRY_RANGE.test(range)`. Add a parser test with the patched-git entry above, expecting `unpublished: true`, beside the existing patched-npm case at test/parsers/yarn-berry.test.ts:233.

## Resolution
yarn-berry.ts fromRegistry() decides a patch by the URL-encoded source after `patch:<name>@` (registry only for npm: / npm%3A, scoped names handled); no decodeURIComponent, so a malformed escape cannot throw. Tests: patched scoped registry package published; patched git and file packages unpublished; existing patched-npm test still passes. Proven: reverting to /^(?:npm|patch):/ fails the git case.
title: Yarn Berry treats every patch: package as published, so a patched git or file package is looked up on the registry

AUD:B0. errors-e18d7a96 moved unresolved lookups into the JSON object because a stderr-only warning let a script read an incomplete analysis as clean, and the comment at 333-334 says so. ## Problem

AUD:S11. `ResolveResult.failures` is `string[]` of `name@version (reason)`, built in five places (client.ts:210, 222, 268, 317, 372), and the CLI emits it verbatim as the JSON `unresolved` array (cli.ts:337). client.ts:67-68: ``/** What failed and why, as `name@version (reason)` */ failures: string[]``. client.ts:268: ``context.failures.push(`${name}@latest (no version in response)`)``. README.md:136-137 documents the entries "as `name@version (reason)`".

Every JSON consumer reimplements a fragile parser, and any later change to the reason wording breaks them without a type or shape change to signal it.

## Fix

Make failures `{ name: string; version: string; reason: string }[]`, with `version: 'latest'` for /latest lookups. Format them as text only in `warnUnresolved` (cli.ts:172-178). Emit the objects in JSON and update README.md:136-137. Adjust the CLI tests that match `unresolved` strings to the object form. Ship it in the same 6.0.0 release.

registry/client.ts exports Failure {name, version, reason} (version 'latest' for /latest); all failure sites build objects; cli.ts formats them only in warnUnresolved (stderr text unchanged) and emits objects in JSON. README documents the shape; audit-cd19913e's breaking note names it. Client tests compare through a labels() helper; new test asserts the raw object for a scoped package; CLI JSON tests assert objects. Proven: pushing strings again fails the structure test.
title: JSON unresolved entries are prose strings that scripts must parse, and the only free time to structure them is this major release

## Problem

AUD:S8. The cache stores are written only by `flushCache()` at the end of `main()` (line 341) or in its `catch` (line 350). Nothing handles SIGINT or SIGTERM, so Ctrl-C, or a CI job cancelled for its timeout, kills the process with every fetched manifest still only in memory. Version manifests never expire, so each of them would have saved a request on every later run.

## Evidence

`grep -rn "SIGINT\|SIGTERM\|process.on(" src/` finds nothing. Reproduced against a local registry (npm_config_registry, 50 ms per response) with a 200-package lockfile and an empty XDG_CACHE_HOME: SIGINT after 1.5 s, by which time the server had answered 200 requests, ended the child with `signal=SIGINT`, and `versions.json` did not exist.

## Impact

The runs most likely to be interrupted are cold runs on large lockfiles, which take minutes (see audit-3b345df5). Each interruption throws away all the progress, so the retry starts from zero.

## Fix

In src/cli.ts, register handlers before the registry pass: `for (const signal of ['SIGINT', 'SIGTERM'] as const) process.once(signal, () => { warnOnFlushFailure(flushCache()); process.exit(signal === 'SIGINT' ? 130 : 143) })`. flushCache is synchronous and never throws, so it is safe here. Add a CLI test that spawns a run against a slow local server, sends SIGINT once requests have been served, and asserts versions.json exists and the exit code is 130.

## Resolution
cli.ts flushOnSignal() registers SIGINT (exit 130) and SIGTERM (exit 143) handlers that flush the cache before exiting. CLI test: against a registry answering only p0, SIGINT after both p0 answers gives exit 130 and versions.json holding p0. Proven: removing the handlers fails it.
title: Interrupting a run discards every registry response fetched so far, because the cache is flushed only at exit paths SIGINT skips

AUD:S17. CONTRIBUTING.md:9-10 sends reporters to this template. It is GitHub's generic web-app template: "Go to '...' / Click on '....'", screenshots, "Desktop: OS, Browser" and "Smartphone: Device, Browser". ## Problem

AUD:B2. .claude/rules/no-silent-degradation.md: "Never drop a constraint, skip a lookup or narrow a mode without a stderr warning or an error." `yarnBerryInstallSets` reads each workspace member's manifest with `readProjectManifest(memberDir).deps ?? {}`, which discards the error. A malformed or missing member package.json makes every one of that member's dependencies production, with no message, so `--no-dev` is quietly not applied to that member. Yarn Classic fails the run in the same situation (yarn-classic.ts:153-161, audit-17da5b1f), and README.md:76-78 documents only Classic's behaviour.

## Evidence

yarn-berry.ts:181: `const manifest = readProjectManifest(memberDir).deps ?? {}`. Reproduced: a Berry lockfile with workspace `m` depending on `a` (peer react ^18) and `d` (peer react ^17), and m's package.json naming `a` in dependencies and `d` in devDependencies but missing its closing brace. `--offline --no-dev --json` reports react ranges for both `a` and `d`, a conflict, and stderr says nothing about the manifest. With the brace restored, the same run reports only `a`.

## Impact

A broken member manifest makes `--no-dev` report dev-only constraints as production ones, including false conflicts and needlessly narrow safe ranges, with nothing to say the filter was skipped.

## Fix

Treat it as Classic does (yarn-classic.ts:155-159): destructure `{ deps, error }` from `readProjectManifest(memberDir)` and, when `deps === null`, throw the same "--no-dev needs a readable package.json in <memberDir>: <error>" message. Update the docstring at 155-157 and README.md:76-78 to say both Yarn formats need every member manifest. Add a test in test/graph/index.test.ts with a malformed member manifest, expecting the throw.

## Resolution
yarn-berry.ts throws '--no-dev needs a readable package.json in <memberDir>[: error]' for an unusable workspace member, as Yarn Classic does; docstring and README updated (both Yarn formats need every member manifest). The test that encoded the old fallback became 'refuses a workspace whose package.json is missing'; new test reproduces the malformed member; the sibling-workspace fixture gained the manifest a real workspace has. Proven: disabling the throw fails the malformed-member test.
title: Yarn Berry --no-dev silently keeps a workspace member's dev dependencies when its package.json is unusable

## Problem

AUD:B0. For yarn-classic, `filterDevPackages` runs after the registry pass (line 295), but `failures`, `skipped` and `latestUncached` were computed over the unfiltered list and are never narrowed. The warnings and the JSON `unresolved` array therefore name packages that are not in the analysis, and say that the ranges "may be too permissive" because of them.

## Evidence

Lines 295-297 replace `packages` with the filtered list. `warnUnresolved(..., failures)` at 301-306, the `skipped` report at 307-312, the `latestUncached` report at 315-320 and the JSON at 337 all use the pre-filter values. Reproduced with a yarn.lock holding `a@^1.0.0` and `b@^1.0.0`, and a package.json naming `a` in dependencies and `b` in devDependencies, run as `--offline --no-dev --json` with an empty cache: `unresolved` is `["a@1.0.0 (no metadata)","b@1.0.0 (no metadata)"]`, stderr says "2 package(s) have no metadata offline" and "latest data is not cached for 2 package(s)", yet only `a` is analysed.

The warning that the ranges may be too permissive fires, and scripts reading `unresolved` treat the result as incomplete, even when every package actually analysed resolved.

After the post-registry filter, keep only failures for surviving packages: build ``const kept = new Set(packages.map(p => `${p.name}@${p.version}`))`` and `const names = new Set(packages.map(p => p.name))`, then `failures = failures.filter(f => { const label = f.slice(0, f.indexOf(' (')); return kept.has(label) || names.has(label.slice(0, label.lastIndexOf('@'))) })`. The name check keeps `name@latest` entries. Recount `latestUncached` the same way. Add the reproduction above as a CLI test expecting only `a` in `unresolved`.

## Resolution
After the post-registry Yarn Classic filter, cli.ts narrows failures (by name@version; latest failures by name), skipped and latestUncached to the kept packages; client returns skipped and latestUncached as package lists for this. CLI tests: offline reproduction reports only `a` and latestUncached 1; online keeps a's latest failure; a stalled registry whose unlooked-up package is the dev one reports skipped 0. Proven: reverting the failure filter and the skipped filter each fail their test.

## Problem

AUD:S20 (type overstatement that mis-versions a release). @ivuorinen/semantic-release-config releases `chore(deps)` as a patch (`{ type: "chore", scope: "deps", release: "patch" }`). The shared Renovate preset now separates its scopes: `dev-deps`, `tooling` and `actions` release nothing, and `deps` is used for runtime dependencies. Dependabot security updates still run, with no `.github/dependabot.yml` to configure them, and title their PRs `chore(deps): ...` whatever the dependency type. This package's runtime closure is only `semver` and `yaml`, neither with dependencies, so every such PR is dev-only, yet squash-merging it under its title cuts a release. The repository's own policy (CONTRIBUTING.md:80-81) is that dev-dependency changes are not user-facing.

## Evidence

Open PR #145 "chore(deps): bump the npm_and_yarn group across 1 directory with 2 updates" bumps brace-expansion 1.1.18 → 1.1.21 and esbuild 0.27.7 → 0.28.2, both dev-only (`npm ls --omit=dev --all` lists only semver and yaml). `ls .github/dependabot.yml` finds no file. Past Dependabot merges carry the same prefix: 5796480 "chore(deps): bump markdown-it and @ivuorinen/markdownlint-config (#102)", 810eff9 "chore(deps): bump tar and npm (#101)". node_modules/@ivuorinen/semantic-release-config/index.cjs:17 holds the patch rule.

## Impact

Each merged Dependabot PR publishes an npm release identical in behaviour to the last, which notifies every dependent and dilutes the changelog. This is the release noise the Renovate scopes were changed to stop.

## Fix

Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with `version: 2`, an `npm` entry for `/` with `schedule: { interval: weekly }`, `open-pull-requests-limit: 0` (security updates only), `commit-message: { prefix: "chore(deps)", prefix-development: "chore(dev-deps)" }`, and security-update groups split by type (`groups: { runtime: { applies-to: security-updates, dependency-type: production }, dev: { applies-to: security-updates, dependency-type: development } }`). Dependabot already titles a lone dev bump `chore(deps-dev)` (a610bfc), but a group mixing types takes the production prefix, as #145 did. A real `semver` or `yaml` fix keeps `chore(deps)` and its patch release. Alternatively, disable Dependabot security updates in the repository settings and rely on Renovate's `vulnerabilityAlerts`, which use the preset's scopes. Retitle PR #145 `chore(dev-deps): ...` before merging.

## Resolution
New .github/dependabot.yml: npm, open-pull-requests-limit 0 (security updates only; Renovate keeps version updates), commit-message prefix chore(deps) / prefix-development chore(dev-deps), security-update groups split by dependency type so a mixed group no longer takes the production prefix. Validated with v8r against schemastore's dependabot-2.0 schema. Open PR #145 still carries its old title; retitling it is the user's action.
title: Dependabot titles dev-only security bumps chore(deps):, which the release rules publish as a patch with no user-facing change

## Problem

AUD:S4. For every entry in `target.ranges`, `renderTarget` runs `allPackages.find(p => p.name === entry.package && p.version === entry.version)` to get the row's latest-version fallback. That is O(ranges × packages) per target, repeated for node, the package manager and each peer target.

## Evidence

table.ts:210: `const own = allPackages.find(p => p.name === entry.package && p.version === entry.version)`. Measured with `renderOutput` on synthetic packages, 40% declaring engines.node: 5,000 packages (2,000 rows) render in 38 ms, and 20,000 packages (8,000 rows) in 874 ms, 23x slower for 4x the input, for the node target alone. `analyzeEngines` on the same 20,000 packages takes 276 ms, so rendering becomes the slowest analysis step.

## Impact

Large monorepo lockfiles (the pnpm parser's comments cite 20,000 packages) spend around a second per target just laying out the table.

## Fix

Build the lookup once per `renderTarget`: ``const byId = new Map(allPackages.map(p => [`${p.name}@${p.version}`, p]))`` and use ``byId.get(`${entry.package}@${entry.version}`)``. Add a test in test/output/table.test.ts that renders a target whose matching package sits last in a long list and still shows its latest version.

## Resolution
table.ts builds one name@version Map per target instead of a find per row. Re-measured: 20,000 packages render in 18 ms (was 874 ms). Test counts element reads through a Proxy: 1,000 declaring packages stay within 2,000 reads and the last package still shows its latest version. Proven: restoring find fails the bounded-reads test.
title: Table rendering scans the whole package list once per declaring package, quadratic in lockfile size

## Problem

AUD:S16 (unsound cast at a trust boundary). `readProjectManifest` returns `JSON.parse(raw) as PackageDeps` without checking any field. `PackageDeps.workspaces` is typed `string[] | { packages?: string[] }`, so `projectManifests` (yarn-classic.ts:146) trusts that `workspaces.packages` is an array and calls `.flatMap` on it. A manifest with `"workspaces": { "packages": "packages/*" }`, an easy mistake for the array form, reaches that call as a string. The resulting TypeError is classed as a bug by `isBug` and printed with a full stack, instead of the one-line "--no-dev needs a readable package.json" message the same function gives for other unusable manifests.

## Evidence

detect.ts:25: `return { deps: JSON.parse(raw) as PackageDeps, error: null }`. yarn-classic.ts:146-147: `const patterns = Array.isArray(workspaces) ? workspaces : (workspaces?.packages ?? [])` then `patterns.flatMap(pattern => ...)`. Reproduced: a yarn.lock with `a@^1.0.0` and package.json `{"workspaces":{"packages":"packages/*"},"dependencies":{"a":"^1.0.0"}}`, run as `--offline --no-dev`, prints `TypeError: patterns.flatMap is not a function` / `at projectManifests (…/src/parsers/yarn-classic.ts:147:28)` and exits 1. The same unchecked-cast class produced audit-30a9ca4c in the npm parser.

## Impact

A plausible manifest typo surfaces as an apparent crash report rather than a message naming the field.

## Fix

In projectManifests, accept only string arrays and fail clearly otherwise: `const raw = Array.isArray(workspaces) ? workspaces : workspaces?.packages ?? []`, then ``if (!Array.isArray(raw) || !raw.every(p => typeof p === 'string')) throw new Error(`--no-dev cannot read the workspaces field of ${join(projectDir, 'package.json')}`)``. Add a test in test/graph/index.test.ts with the string form, expecting that message and no TypeError.

## Resolution
yarn-classic.ts projectManifests accepts only a list of string patterns (array, or object.packages) and otherwise throws '--no-dev cannot read the workspaces field of <path>'; a string workspaces is refused instead of read as none. Tests: object with packages read; string under packages, plain string and a non-string entry refused without a TypeError. Proven: disabling the check fails the string-under-packages test.
title: package.json is cast to PackageDeps unchecked, so a string workspaces.packages crashes Yarn Classic --no-dev with a stack trace

## Problem

Manual sweep (gating intent). `VALIDATE_ALL_CODEBASE` is `${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}`, and the comment says "Validates all source when push on main, else just the git diff with main". The workflow triggers only on `pull_request` and `workflow_call`, and no workflow calls it (`grep -rn "pr-lint" .github` finds no `uses:`), so `github.event_name` is never `push`. MegaLinter's file-level linters therefore only ever see the files a PR changes. A file that went in while a linter was disabled, or before one was added or upgraded, is never re-checked.

## Evidence

pr-lint.yml:4-7: `on:` / `pull_request:` / `branches: [main]` / `workflow_call: {}`. Line 67: `VALIDATE_ALL_CODEBASE: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}`. Lines 64-66 carry the comment. The only `uses:` of a local workflow in .github is publish.yml:18 calling ci.yml.

## Impact

The comment promises a periodic full lint of main that never runs, so lint debt in untouched files accumulates invisibly. The dead `workflow_call` trigger (also on stale.yml) suggests callers that do not exist.

## Fix

Pick one: add `push: branches: [main]` to pr-lint.yml's `on:`, which keeps the job read-only, so the expression becomes reachable and main is fully linted after each merge; or set `VALIDATE_ALL_CODEBASE: false` and replace the comment with "Lints only the files a pull request changes." Remove the unused `workflow_call: {}` triggers from pr-lint.yml and stale.yml either way.

## Resolution
pr-lint.yml sets VALIDATE_ALL_CODEBASE: false with an accurate comment (lints only files a PR changes), and the unused workflow_call triggers are removed from pr-lint.yml and stale.yml (`gh search code` found no callers of either). actionlint and zizmor --pedantic report 0.
title: MegaLinter's full-codebase mode can never switch on: the workflow has no push trigger and nothing calls it

## Problem

AUD:S23 (locale-unsafe sort). `computeIntersection` breaks ties between ranges with equal minimum versions using `a.range.localeCompare(b.range)`, commented "Equal minimums fall back to the text, or input order would pick the first seed". `localeCompare` without a locale argument collates by the process's default locale and ICU version, so the same lockfile can sort its seeds differently on two machines. Range text is protocol data, not prose, and its order has no reason to follow a locale.

## Evidence

intersect.ts:220: `return semver.compare(minA, minB) || a.range.localeCompare(b.range)`. Measured on Node 26.10.0 (ICU 78.3): `new Intl.Collator('da').compare('x', 'X')` is 1, while 'en', 'sv', 'tr', 'lt', 'ja', 'zh', 'fi', 'cs', 'et' and 'haw' give -1, so a LANG=da_DK run orders those two ranges the other way round. No outcome change was constructed: `x` and `X` normalise to the same range, and a flip that changes the conflict set needs case-differing prerelease bounds plus a third range overlapping only one of them.

## Impact

Hardening only today. The comment states an ordering guarantee that the code does not keep across environments, which matters if the result is ever compared between a developer machine and CI.

## Fix

Compare code units, which is locale-free and cheaper: `return semver.compare(minA, minB) || (a.range < b.range ? -1 : a.range > b.range ? 1 : 0)`. The existing tie-break test in test/analyzer/intersect.test.ts should keep passing; add one pinning the order of `^18.0.0` and `>=18`, which compare differently by code point (`>` before `^`) than by collation.

## Resolution
intersect.ts breaks equal-minimum ties by code unit (Number(a > b) - Number(a < b)), not localeCompare. Test: conflicts `<1.0.0-Alpha` and `<1.0.0-alpha` (equal minimums) are reported upper first, the code-unit order; English collation gives the reverse. Proven: restoring localeCompare fails it.
title: The seed tie-break uses localeCompare, so its "deterministic" order depends on the user's locale
