## Problem

Weak assertion where a stronger one is checkable. The guard exists because Node's coverage merge can drop a never-taken branch range (tests-3ef69c7f). It records branches as the `file:line` strings `all` and `zero`, and flags a partial-run zero only when the full run has no BRDA entry on that line at all. If the merge drops a zero-count range on a line that also holds another branch range, such as one arm of a one-line `a ? b : c` or `x ?? y`, the surviving range keeps `file:line` in `full.all`, the drop is not reported, and `npm run cov`'s 100% branch gate passes without the branch having run.

## Evidence

coverage-merge-guard.mjs:54-56: `const [lineNumber, , , count] = line.slice(5).split(',')` / ``all.add(`${file}:${lineNumber}`)`` / ``if (count === '0') zero.add(`${file}:${lineNumber}`)``. Line 68: `const hidden = [...partial.zero].filter(key => !full.all.has(key))`. The current tree passes (the guard printed "No never-taken branch is hidden by the coverage merge."), so this is hardening, not a hidden branch found today.

## Impact

The 100% branch figure the project relies on, with CONTRIBUTING.md:51-61 describing this guard as the backstop, can over-report on exactly the dense one-line branches TypeScript code uses most.

## Fix

Count BRDA entries per line instead of recording presence: build `Map<string, number>` for both runs, and treat a line as hidden when the partial run had a zero-count branch there and `full.get(key) ?? 0` is less than `partial.get(key)`. The full run executes a superset of the partial run, so V8 reports at least as many ranges per line, and only a merge drop lowers the count. Prove it fails by stubbing the full lcov in a scratch run with one of two BRDA lines removed, then restore.

## Resolution
coverage-merge-guard.mjs counts BRDA entries per line (readBranches) and flags a line where the partial run had a never-taken branch and the full run has fewer entries. Proof with synthetic lcov: partial two branches on line 10 (one zero), full with the zero arm dropped -> flagged (old presence check: not flagged); full with both arms -> not flagged. On the real tree the stricter guard passes.
title: The coverage-merge guard keys branches by line, so a dropped branch that shares a line with a surviving one passes unnoticed

## Problem

Incorrect. src/types.ts:39 documents `intersection` as "Computed safe range for installed versions; null if conflict", and :47 says the same for `latestIntersection`. The interface is the `--json` targets contract.

## Evidence

computeIntersection returns `{ intersection: null, conflicts: [], invalid }` when no valid range is left (src/analyzer/intersect.ts:247-249). analyzeTarget keeps a target whenever either side has ranges (src/analyzer/intersect.ts:351). So a target where only the latest releases declare a constraint, or where every installed range is invalid semver, has `intersection: null` with an empty `conflicts`. The same holds for `latestIntersection` when only installed versions declare one.

## Impact

A script that treats `intersection === null` as a conflict, as the field doc says, reports a conflict for a target whose installed versions declare nothing. The CI gate proposed in docs-629e9d0b would have failed clean trees this way.

## Fix

src/types.ts:39 → "Computed safe range for installed versions; null on a conflict (see conflicts) or when no installed version declares a valid range". src/types.ts:47 → the same for latest versions (see latestConflicts). Test for conflicts with `conflicts.length > 0`.

## Resolution
AnalysisTarget.intersection and latestIntersection docs now say null means a conflict (see conflicts or latestConflicts) or no valid declared range. README's JSON section says to test the conflict lists, not null.
title: AnalysisTarget says intersection is "null if conflict"; it is also null when that side has no valid range

## Problem

Incorrect. README.md:71 says "Exit codes: `0` success, `1` unrecoverable error." The `--help` text at src/cli.ts:112 says the same: "Exit codes: 0 success, 1 unrecoverable error".

## Evidence

src/cli.ts:251-252 calls `flushOnSignal('SIGINT', 130)` and `flushOnSignal('SIGTERM', 143)`. flushOnSignal (src/cli.ts:234-239) flushes the cache, then calls `process.exit(code)`. Before this branch, a signal killed the process without an exit code of its own; now the CLI exits with these two codes itself.

## Impact

A CI job cancelled at its timeout gets SIGTERM and sees 143. A script that branches on the documented contract treats it as unknown. The docs also leave out that the cache is saved on interrupt, which explains why a re-run after Ctrl-C is faster.

## Fix

README.md:71 → "Exit codes: `0` success, `1` unrecoverable error, `130` interrupted (SIGINT), `143` terminated (SIGTERM). Both signals save the cache first." Apply the same change to the help text at src/cli.ts:112, then update any test that asserts the help output.

## Resolution
README exit codes add 130 (SIGINT) and 143 (SIGTERM) and note that both save the cache first. The --help text lists 130 and 143 and says success includes conflicts. No test asserts the help text.
title: README and --help list exit codes 0 and 1 only; an interrupted run exits 130 or 143

A user with an npm or pnpm lockfile, no node_modules and an empty cache expects `--offline` to resolve nothing. It resolves installed constraints from the lockfile. The option row also contradicts the README's own "How it works" section.

## Fix

README.md:63 → "Skip registry lookups; use the lockfile, `node_modules` and the cache only". src/cli.ts:104 → "Skip registry; use lockfile, node_modules and cache only" (column width permitting), then update any test that asserts the help output.

The README option row and the --help line for --offline now name the lockfile alongside node_modules and the cache.
title: --offline is documented as "node_modules and cache only" but also uses lockfile metadata

The README registry paragraph adds `not from a registry`, `no metadata` (offline, with nothing cached and no lockfile constraints) and `no version in response` to the failure reasons.
title: README presents four failure reasons as the full set; --json unresolved entries carry three more

## Problem

Missing. README.md:34-36 lists "running constraint checks in CI" as a use, and README.md:71 gives exit codes as "`0` success, `1` unrecoverable error". Nothing says whether a conflict, an unresolved lookup or a skipped package changes the exit code, or how a CI job should gate on them.

## Evidence

src/cli.ts:396-403 prints the table or JSON and returns. Conflicts (`conflicts` and `latestConflicts` on each target), `unresolved`, `skipped` and `latestUncached` never reach `process.exit`. Only the top-level error handler at src/cli.ts:405-413 exits 1. A run where every target conflicts exits 0.

## Impact

A CI step `npx @ivuorinen/semver-ranger` passes on a conflicting tree, which is the case it was added to catch. The user discovers this only when a conflict ships.

## Fix

Add after the exit-codes line (README.md:71, see docs-31875606): "Conflicts, unresolved lookups and skipped packages are results, not errors, and exit `0`. To fail CI on them, read `--json`, for example: `semver-ranger --json | node -e 'const a = JSON.parse(require(\"fs\").readFileSync(0)); process.exit(a.targets.some(t => t.intersection === null) || a.unresolved.length > 0 ? 1 : 0)'`." `intersection` is `string | null`, "null if conflict" (AnalysisTarget in src/types.ts).

## Resolution
README says conflicts, unresolved lookups and skipped packages exit 0, and the JSON section has a CI gate snippet. The snippet tests `conflicts.length > 0`, not `intersection === null` (docs-8850a26b). Verified: it exits 0 on this repo's own clean output and 1 on a planted conflict.
title: README offers CI constraint checks but never says a conflict exits 0, so CI must read --json

Someone checking whether a deletion route is covered reads the header and concludes that unlink, xargs and find -delete pass unchecked, then adds a duplicate guard or files a false gap.

The deleted-path-refs header now lists every gated form: rm, unlink, mv, their git forms including git -C, xargs rm, and find -delete or -exec rm.

## Problem

Tone (in scope for this run at the user's request: nitpicker documentation tone, no compliments or filler). README.md:30 is headed "Why it's useful". Lines 34-36 say "`semver-ranger` does it in one command, making it useful for deciding which Node.js version to target, validating that a new package won't break your peer dependency setup, and running constraint checks in CI." Line 40 says "The quickest way is to run it without installing:".

## Evidence

The heading and "making it useful for" praise the tool instead of naming its uses, and the uses sit in a trailing participle clause. "The quickest way" is a comparison nothing in the README backs, and it adds nothing to the command that follows. The rest of the README (Usage, JSON output, Private registries, Cache) is declarative and specific, so these lines stand out.

## Impact

No functional risk. The first screen of the npm page reads as marketing copy, and the three uses are harder to scan than a list.

## Fix

README.md:30-36 → heading "## When to use it", then "Tracing transitive `engines` and peer dependency constraints by hand stops working once a project has more than a handful of dependencies. Use `semver-ranger` to:" followed by three bullets: "pick the Node.js version to target", "check that a new package fits your peer dependency setup", "run constraint checks in CI". Do not write "fail CI on a conflict": a run with conflicts exits 0 (src/cli.ts:396-403 prints and returns; only errors exit 1), so a CI check has to read `--json`. README.md:40 → "Run it without installing:".

## Resolution
"Why it's useful" is now "When to use it" with three bullets, and "The quickest way is" is now "Run it without installing". The CI bullet points to the JSON section instead of claiming conflicts fail CI.
title: README's "Why it's useful" and Install intro use self-promotion and filler instead of stating what the tool is for

The feature request template asks for Problem (command, lockfile format, what the output lacks), Proposal and Alternatives, in place of GitHub's default text.
